works.title: Author Correction: Serine protease inhibitor A3 is a soluble SIRPα ligand that suppresses inflammation and antitumor immunity
Macrophage NOX4/ROS–NLRP3 signaling and metabolic reprogramming in gastric premalignant lesions: microbial extracellular vesicles as candidate persistent triggers
works.abstract: Gastric carcinogenesis proceeds through a multistep cascade in which chronic Helicobacter pylori infection drives chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG), spasmolytic polypeptide-expressing metaplasia (SPEM), intestinal metaplasia (IM), and dysplasia before invasive adenocarcinoma emerges. Although H. pylori eradication lowers cancer incidence, a substantial residual risk persists in successfully treated individuals, and metachronous gastric cancer continues to arise within a field of atrophic and metaplastic mucosa. This review examines the contribution of macrophages to this residual risk, focusing on a signaling axis in which inducible NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4)–derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) licenses glycolytic reprogramming that supports NLRP3 inflammasome activation and sustained IL-1β release. We discuss how bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs), including H. pylori outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) and vesicles shed by a dysregulated gastric microbiota, may provide a protected source of microbial stimuli that could help maintain this program after the original pathogen has been cleared; whether H. pylori-derived vesicles persist after eradication, or are replaced by vesicles produced de novo by the residual non-H. pylori microbiota, has not been determined. We further consider trained immunity as a working framework for persistent macrophage responsiveness, distinguishing short-lived priming of circulating monocytes from durable tissue or progenitor memory, while noting that direct evidence for gastric mucosal trained immunity remains limited. The downstream consequences for chief-cell transdifferentiation into SPEM, stromal remodeling, and the gradual loss ofprotective folate receptor β (FOLR2)-positivemacrophages are reviewed, together with the therapeutic implications of NOX4-directed inhibition, NLRP3 blockade, and metabolic interference. We conclude that intervening on the macrophage NOX4/ROS–metabolic–NLRP3 axis, rather than on bacterial burden alone, may help address the residual gastric cancer risk that persists after H. pylori eradication.

works.title: The oral-gut immune axis: a bidirectional hypothesis of the oral cavity as an immune programming hub for systemic and gut mucosal immunity
works.abstract: The oral cavity has long been viewed simply as the site of food intake. Research in recent years has shown that the oral mucosa is a site of chronic low-grade inflammation that continuously produces inflammatory mediators. Given its specific structure, microbial products and immune mediators in the oral cavity can enter the bloodstream, while swallowed saliva continuously delivers oral microorganisms and their products to the gut. Oral dysbiosis, particularly in periodontitis, has been associated with systemic immune reprogramming, including trained immunity of monocytes, neutrophil priming, and expansion of gut-homing T helper 17 (Th17) cells. These modifications may contribute to intestinal barrier dysfunction, alterations in gut microbiota composition, and an increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. However, current evidence is largely associative: the presence of oral bacteria in intestinal tissue does not establish that they initiate intestinal disease, and an inflamed gut may itself favor the colonization of oral-derived taxa. Bidirectional influences between oral and gut inflammation therefore cannot be excluded, and reverse causation remains plausible. Genetic studies have identified polymorphisms in genes of innate immunity, such as nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2), interleukin-23 receptor (IL23R), and the interleukin-1 gene cluster (IL1 cluster), in both periodontitis and gastrointestinal diseases. However, because these loci are highly pleiotropic and have been associated with multiple inflammatory disorders affecting different organs, shared susceptibility genes alone cannot distinguish a genuine oral-to-gut axis from independent diseases sharing common immune-related genetic architecture. We propose the Oral-Gut Immune Axis (OGIA) here as a testable hypothesis, not as an established paradigm. OGIA is a predominantly, but not exclusively, oral-to-gut directional model that positions the oral cavity as a potential immune programming hub. Under specific genetic and microbial conditions, periodontal inflammation may act as an upstream contributor to gastrointestinal pathology. This framework generates testable predictions and identifies oral-targeted interventions as candidate preventive strategies, while acknowledging that current evidence remains insufficient to establish causality. Accordingly, the OGIA framework does not claim that microbial translocation is a demonstrated cause of human gastrointestinal disease. It treats translocation as one candidate mechanism among several, to be discriminated from systemic immune signaling in future studies.

works.title: Nutrient-derived metabolic signals in tumor immune regulation: bioavailability, compartmental allocation, and translational boundaries
works.abstract: The relationship between dietary factors and antitumor immunity has attracted growing attention, but dietary intake, circulating biomarkers, and biological activity within tumor-associated tissues occupy different positions along the path from exposure to function. Nutrient signals are continually reshaped by host processing and local delivery. Their effects depend less on the nutrient label itself than on the molecular form that reaches a given cell and the function that is actually limiting in that cell. This review integrates mechanistic and clinical evidence to explain why the same nutritional change may preserve effector-cell function or support tumor adaptation, with opposing compartment-specific effects most clearly demonstrated for lipid-related pathways. We also distinguish interventions that directly act on tumor-immune processes from nutritional support strategies designed mainly to maintain patient reserve and treatment tolerance. Claims of immune regulation should match the level of measurement. When tumor cells and immune cells may respond differently, paired compartment-specific readouts are needed. Nutritional strategies have translational value only when they target a defined and reversible limitation in a specific patient group and treatment window.

works.title: Outcomes of CAR T cell therapy in diffuse large B cell lymphoma transformed from follicular lymphoma: a single center retrospective analysis
works.abstract: Introduction Follicular lymphoma (FL) transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) confers chemotherapy resistance and poor prognosis. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed treatment of aggressive large B-cell lymphoma, yet outcomes in transformed FL (tFL) remain incompletely characterized. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective analysis of 30 consecutive patients with tFL who received CAR T-cell therapy. Twenty-six patients (87%) received CD19 CAR T cells; four received alternative products (CD20-targeted, CD19/CD20 dual-targeted, or CD19/CD22 bispecific) based on individualized clinical reasoning. Results Median age was 52 years; 97% had stage 3-4 disease, 40% had bone marrow involvement, and 33% had transformed double-hit lymphoma (DHL). Among 25 patients with available tumor tissue, frequently mutated genes included CREBBP (60%), KMT2D (56%), and TP53 (56%). At median follow-up of 30.5 months, median progression-free survival (PFS) was 11 months and median overall survival (OS) was not reached; 2-year PFS and OS rates were 46.7% and 63.2%, respectively. No patient developed grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome (CRS) or grade ≥3 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS); however, grade 4 cytopenias and infections were common. In exploratory analyses, ECOG PS >1, bone marrow involvement, DHL, and non-complete remission (non-CR) status at 3 months were associated with inferior OS in univariate analysis. Discussion Multivariable estimates were limited by small event numbers and wide confidence intervals; non-CR status at 3 months and DHL were associated with inferior outcomes in exploratory analyses but should not be regarded as definitively established independent prognostic factors. The high frequency of TP53, CREBBP, and KMT2D mutations underscores the distinct molecular biology of transformed disease; these molecular findings are descriptive and require validation.

works.title: Eosinophils in non-small cell lung cancer immunotherapy: from dual clinical associations and antitumor mechanisms to a prospective validation framework
works.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are an important treatment for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the lack of reliable biomarkers for outcome stratification limits their precise clinical application. Peripheral blood eosinophil-related parameters, including absolute eosinophil count (AEC), relative eosinophil count (REC) and dynamic changes during treatment, have been studied as candidate biomarkers in recent years because of their convenient detection and dynamic monitoring. At the same time, tumor tissue eosinophilia (TATE), as a direct manifestation of a local immune response, has also attracted attention. This review focuses on the clinical associations of the above indicators in the immunotherapy of NSCLC: the association between baseline AEC and REC levels and patient survival, the association of early on-treatment eosinophil elevation with clinical benefit, the association between baseline AEC and immune-related adverse events, particularly checkpoint inhibitor-related pneumonitis, and whether TATE may provide supplementary information to peripheral blood indicators. In addition, the potential role of eosinophils in the association of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) with efficacy is explored, raising the hypothesis that eosinophils may lie at the intersection of antitumor immunity and immune-mediated toxicity. Based on the available evidence, we further propose a framework for prospective validation that incorporates prespecified baseline stratification, early on-treatment dynamic monitoring, endpoint assessment, and multivariable modeling, with the aim of facilitating the transition of eosinophil-related biomarkers from retrospective associations to prospective clinical validation. In addition to clinical evidence, this paper also summarizes the potential mechanisms through which eosinophils are recruited, activated, and participate in antitumor immunity within the tumor microenvironment. Existing evidence suggests that the above indicators have potential clinical utility, but problems such as inconsistent cut-off values, lack of standardization of dynamic monitoring, and insufficient prospective verification have not yet been resolved. The NSCLC-specific mechanisms underlying eosinophil-associated effects require further investigation.

works.title: Neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage: immune cell dynamics, molecular networks, and therapeutic implications
works.abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke subtype whose functional outcome is largely determined by secondary brain injury rather than by the mass effect of the hematoma alone. A growing body of evidence places immune-cell-mediated neuroinflammation at the center of this secondary injury. Following vascular rupture, blood-derived damage-associated molecular patterns, heme, thrombin, and complement rapidly activate resident microglia and recruit circulating leukocytes, establishing a spatiotemporally dynamic inflammatory microenvironment. Microglia are among the earliest responders and exhibit a spectrum of functional states ranging from pro-inflammatory to reparative and phagocytic, in which the NLRP3 inflammasome and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling act as pivotal amplification hubs. Infiltrating neutrophils and their neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) aggravate blood–brain barrier disruption and perihematomal edema, forming mutually amplifying feedback loops with microglia and with the complement system. Monocyte-derived macrophages subsequently dominate hematoma clearance and inflammation resolution, while T and B lymphocytes and the complement cascade further shape the evolving immune response. Systemic inflammatory indices such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio hold prognostic value but are limited by sampling heterogeneity and by the distinction between association, incremental prediction, and treatment guidance. We argue that the biphasic, cell-type-specific nature of post-ICH neuroinflammation defines a series of “immune windows” that demands a shift from broad immunosuppression toward phase-specific, cell-specific precision immunomodulation. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are refining this cellular atlas and are poised to guide next-generation, mechanism-anchored, biomarker-informed therapeutic strategies.

works.title: Molecular warning-driven proactive intervention strategies for antibody-mediated rejection in kidney transplantation
works.abstract: The traditional “post-injury salvage” model, which relies on a rise in serum creatinine followed by biopsy confirmation, frequently leads to irreversible graft injury. This narrative review integrates the immunopathological mechanisms of antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) with the limitations of current diagnostic approaches, and proposes a shift in the trigger for clinical decisions from “organ dysfunction” to “molecular signal abnormality.” We organize the review around a Decision Algorithm that follows the logic of pathological mechanisms and diagnostic gaps, biological interpretation of molecular signals, risk stratification, biopsy and treatment decisions, and dynamic monitoring of treatment response. Key biomarkers include donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA), functional donor-specific antibodies (DSA) with C1q-binding status and IgG subclass, and urinary CXCL10. We emphasize that dd-cfDNA should be interpreted as a dynamic injury signal rather than a static threshold, incorporating serial changes, patient-specific baseline, magnitude of change, and duration of elevation. The algorithm explicitly distinguishes pre-existing, de novo , and persistent DSA, and incorporates DSA origin, time of appearance, persistence, changes in MFI, and complement-binding status. Non-HLA antibodies are presented as complementary or exploratory markers in DSA-negative cases, with uncertainties in assay standardization, clinical thresholds, and causal relationship to tissue injury. We present a four-tier risk stratification system with corresponding monitoring and treatment decision pathways. Clinical action plans based on defined biomarker thresholds are specified, with explicit labeling of which thresholds are supported by prospective/multicenter evidence and which are proposed as a future management framework. Targeted therapies—IL-6 blockade, complement-targeted therapy, and FcRn inhibitors—are graded by evidence level (randomized trials, observational studies, case series, or hypothesis-generating proposals) and should be used individually according to biomarker-driven stratification, preferably within clinical trials. Although challenges remain in standardization, cost, accessibility, and the lack of prospective interventional validation, an integrated diagnostic framework combining multi-omics, machine learning, and molecular biopsy holds promise for achieving personalized and prospective post-transplant immune management. This approach may interrupt the chain of injury before fibrosis develops and improve long-term graft survival.

works.title: Immune dysregulation: an “accelerator” of gut resistome expansion and multidrug-resistant organism infection risk in ICU patients
works.abstract: Immune dysregulation is a common and critical condition in intensive care unit (ICU) patients, significantly increasing their susceptibility to infections. Beyond heightened vulnerability, immune dysfunction plays a pivotal role in accelerating the expansion of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) within the gut microbiome, thereby promoting the emergence and proliferation of multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs). This review systematically examines the mechanisms by which immune dysregulation acts as a key “accelerator” driving the amplification of the gut resistome in ICU patients and explores the intrinsic link between this process and the elevated risk of MDRO infections. We analyze multiple dimensions including immune suppression-induced gut microbial imbalance, inflammation-mediated horizontal gene transfer (HGT), antibiotic pressure fostering selective advantages, and clinical intervention strategies. Integrating the latest advances in metagenomics and immunology, this article aims to provide novel theoretical insights and clinical guidance for infection prevention and control in the ICU setting. By elucidating the central role of immune dysregulation in ARG expansion, we emphasize the necessity of precise immune modulation combined with targeted anti-infective approaches to reduce MDRO infection risk and improve patient outcomes in critical care.

works.title: Could dexmedetomidine-induced immunogenic cell death sensitize EBV-driven nasopharyngeal carcinoma to PD-1 blockade? A preclinical hypothesis and falsification framework
works.abstract: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is an Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-driven epithelial malignancy characterized by persistent viral antigens but inefficient antigen presentation, dysfunctional dendritic cells, and exhausted T cells. Although programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade has improved clinical outcomes, many patients do not achieve durable benefit. Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is an alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist used for sedation that was recently reported in a single preclinical study to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) through partial endoplasmic reticulum stress, eIF2α phosphorylation, autophagy, surface calreticulin exposure, and HMGB1 and ATP release, effects that enhanced dendritic-cell uptake and cooperated with PD-1 blockade in non-NPC tumor models. This phenotype requires approximately 600 μM DEX, several orders of magnitude above the concentration range in which DEX engages the alpha2-adrenoceptor selectively, so the effect more likely reflects an off-target interaction than canonical receptor pharmacology. We propose that, if independently reproduced in EBV-positive NPC and traced to a defined molecular target, this phenomenon could enhance cross-presentation of EBV antigens and prime EBV-specific CD8+ T cells, providing an immunological rationale for combination with PD-1 blockade. This hypothesis is constrained by the exposure gap, the absence of independent or NPC-specific validation, context-dependent tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive effects, a DEX-associated T-cell exhaustion signature, and the unresolved identity of the responsible target. We therefore do not advocate systemic dose escalation or immediate interventional testing. Instead, we present a staged falsification framework requiring independent confirmation of canonical ICD, spatially resolved demonstration of antigen-specific cross-presentation and stromal T-cell infiltration, deconvolution of the molecular target through thermal proteomics and CRISPR-based screening, and exclusion of hemodynamic, metastatic, and immunosuppressive liabilities before efficacy testing in EBV-relevant models. Only if these criteria are satisfied should localized delivery, target-directed inducer design, or prospective clinical evaluation be considered. This Perspective repositions DEX as a phenotypic probe for target discovery rather than a repurposed receptor agonist or an established anticancer therapy.

works.title: A host-tumor interaction-based five-dimensional risk stratification system integrating immune surveillance, inflammation, nutrition, coagulation, and tumor burden for prognostic evaluation in stage III colorectal cancer
works.abstract: Objective Stage III colorectal cancer (CRC) exhibits substantial prognostic heterogeneity, underscoring the need for robust risk stratification tools. We aimed to develop and validate a novel five-dimensional (5D) score integrating immune surveillance, inflammation, nutrition, coagulation, and tumor burden to improve prognostic assessment in these patients. Materials and methods We retrospectively enrolled 338 patients with stage III CRC, who were randomly assigned to a discovery cohort (n=228) and a validation cohort (n=110). Preoperative peripheral blood biomarkers were detected before surgery to construct the 5D score. Patients were followed for three years to assess recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS). Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox proportional hazards regression, and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to evaluate the prognostic performance of the score. Results Low levels of the combined lymphocyte-eosinophil-basophil immune- surveillance axis and prealbumin, together with elevated monocyte counts, fibrinogen, and the combined CEA-CA19–9 score, were significantly associated with inferior survival. The 5D score showed a strong stepwise association with both RFS and OS (plog-rank<0.001). Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified the 5D risk stratification system as an independent prognostic factor in both the discovery and validation cohorts and across age-stratified subgroups. Time-dependent ROC analyses demonstrated that the score achieved superior predictive performance for RFS and OS compared with biomarkers representing any single biological dimension. Furthermore, patients with low- and intermediate-risk scores appeared to benefit from the oxaliplatin-plus-capecitabine regimen, whereas those with ultra-high-risk scores experienced poor survival despite standard treatment. Conclusions The 5D score is a simple, cost-effective, and robust prognostic tool for patients with stage III CRC. By integrating complementary dimensions of host-tumor interactions, the 5D score may improve preoperative risk stratification and support individualized postoperative surveillance and treatment decisions. Prospective multi-center studies are warranted to further validate its clinical utility and biological significance.

works.title: CIPHER-Lung: retrospective exploratory internal evaluation and clinical benchmarking of an interpretable peripheral blood immune score for lung cancer prognosis
works.abstract: Background Clinical Immune Phenotyping and Explainable Risk Modeling for Lung Cancer (CIPHER-Lung) is a rule-based peripheral blood immune score that organizes measured biomarkers into clinically readable concepts. We assessed whether these concepts outperform constituent markers, remain stable under assay-like computational perturbations, and identify discordance with standard disease burden. Methods This retrospective exploratory internal evaluation used 260 sample records from de-identified participants in an existing institutional cohort. Overall-survival analyses included 162 patients with lung cancer and 73 deaths, and only 31 had all six markers. The primary available-concept score combined the measured subset of a six-marker panel into four phenotypic proxies: loss of T-cell surveillance, checkpoint activation/terminal differentiation, cytokine inflammation, and hematology/myeloid inflammation. The fixed formula was applied without outcome-based coefficient refitting. Analyses included matched marker comparisons, clinical benchmarking, inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted (IPCW) evaluation, concept ablation, limited adaptation, computational jitter dropout, and 24-month discordance phenotyping. Results The available-concept score had a Harrell C-index of 0.697 and IPCW cumulative/dynamic AUROCs of 0.765 and 0.764 at 12 and 24 months. On matched participants, the composite exceeded CD3, CD8+PD-1+, CD8+CD57+, and the cytokine concept, whereas the NLR/hematology concept performed similarly in its smaller subset. The supplied fixed weighting did not outperform unweighted aggregation. Training-fold calibration and a four-concept linear probe produced only modest gains over the fixed score. Under five-point concept jitter plus 10% dropout, the median C-index was 0.691, rank correlation was 0.939, and high-risk agreement was 0.912. Descriptive point estimates were higher for clinical models. The combined model showed no material point-estimate gain over the clinical model. Paired intervals for clinical-model comparisons were unavailable. Conclusions CIPHER-Lung provides an interpretable immune-state representation supported by this retrospective exploratory internal evaluation. The score is not supported for stand-alone diagnosis, treatment selection, or replacement of stage and performance status. Candidate uses in longitudinal phenotyping, enrichment, or point-of-care reporting require complete-marker multicenter validation, documented reference standards, analytical qualification, external calibration, and prospective impact studies.

works.title: Strain-specific influenza vaccine immunogenicity in adults with severe asthma receiving biologic therapy: a real-world baseline-adjusted HAI study
works.abstract: Background Evidence on influenza vaccine immunogenicity during biologic treatment for severe asthma remains limited, particularly in adults treated in routine clinical practice. Methods In this prospective single-centre observational study, we analysed pre- and post-vaccination haemagglutination-inhibition (HAI) titres in 147 adults with asthma who received Grippol Quadrivalent during the 2023–2024 season: 126 patients with severe asthma receiving ongoing biologic therapy and 21 asthma controls not receiving biologic therapy. Blood was obtained before vaccination and 4–6 weeks after vaccination. For each vaccine strain, log2(post-vaccination HAI) was modelled using analysis of covariance with study group and the corresponding log2(pre-vaccination HAI) titre as predictors. The group coefficient was back-transformed to an adjusted geometric mean ratio (GMR; biologic therapy/control). Results Adjusted GMRs were 0.61 (95% CI 0.33–1.13; P = 0.113) for A/H1N1/Victoria, 1.08 (0.64–1.81; P = 0.779) for A/H3N2/Darwin, 0.46 (0.23–0.94; P = 0.032) for B/Austria, and 0.59 (0.34–1.05; P = 0.073) for B/Phuket. Conclusion Baseline-adjusted estimates differed numerically across strains, but between-strain heterogeneity was not formally tested.B/Austria yielded a nominally lower adjusted titre (P = 0.032; Holm-adjusted P = 0.128), but not after additional adjustment for age and sex (GMR 0.54, 95% CI 0.28–1.05; P = 0.068); confidence intervals for the other three strains included unity; all findings are exploratory. These observational data extend randomized evidence from individual biologics to an adult real-world severe-asthma cohort.

works.title: Immunotherapy initiation timing in multimodal treatment of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: a setting-specific narrative review
works.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have established roles in selected advanced and postoperative esophageal squamous cell carcinoma settings, but evidence supporting an immunotherapy-containing regimen does not necessarily establish its optimal initiation time. This narrative review evaluates timing within advanced, neoadjuvant, postoperative, and definitive chemoradiotherapy pathways. A targeted synthesis of the previously assembled literature through August 2026 was supplemented by separately documented citation and protocol checks; incomplete historical search documentation limits reproducibility. Evidence is classified by study design and whether initiation timing was actually randomized. Phase III trials support first-line chemoimmunotherapy in appropriate advanced-disease populations, whereas the randomized neoadjuvant HCHTOG1906 trial did not demonstrate superior pathological response or survival with cycle-day-3 versus same-day toripalimab. CRISEC and EPOC1802 used post-chemoradiotherapy schedules without randomizing start time. Biological observations and prolonged antibody activity do not identify a transferable calendar window. We propose a research framework that distinguishes established safety requirements, protocol-specific eligibility thresholds, and unvalidated recovery measurements; operationalizes subsequent-treatment completability through prespecified pathway milestones; and separates prognostic, predictive, pharmacodynamic, and safety/readiness biomarkers. Future trials should specify the population, treatment strategies, common time zero, intercurrent-event handling, and primary estimand. Failure to reach assigned treatment must remain visible in intention-to-treat analyses, while survival, disease control, treatment delivery, and patient-reported recovery require setting-specific prioritization. Established stage-specific treatment should remain the clinical reference rather than be displaced by an unvalidated timing strategy.

works.title: IP10 armoring enhances CLDN-18.2–directed CAR-T cell therapy in pancreatic cancer by promoting T cell infiltration and vascular remodeling, with additive benefits from IL-15 co-modification
works.abstract: Introduction Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly malignant tumor with a dismal prognosis, largely due to its desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) that restricts effector T cell infiltration and limits chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy efficacy. Claudin-18.2 (CLDN18.2) is frequently overexpressed in PDAC and represents an attractive therapeutic target. Our previous study demonstrated that IL-15-armored CLDN18.2 CAR-T cells elicit superior antitumor activity in murine models. To further enhance therapeutic efficacy, we investigated whether chemokine modification of CLDN18.2 CAR-T cells could promote tumor infiltration and amplify antitumor activity. Methods The chemokine CXCL10 (IP10) recruits immune cells via CXCR3. We generated CLDN18.2-targeted murine CAR-T cells secreting IP10 alone (H9 CAR-IP10) or in combination with IL-15 (15×10 H9 CAR). Cell phenotypes, cytotoxic activity, and chemotactic capacity were assessed in vitro using flow cytometry, xCELLigence, and Transwell assays. An immunocompetent Panc02-CLDN18.2 subcutaneous tumor model was applied to evaluate in vivo antitumor efficacy, survival, and TME alterations. Results IP10 modification did not affect CAR expression, expansion, phenotype, exhaustion markers, or cytokine secretion. Both H9 CAR T and H9 CAR-IP10 T cells exhibited potent antigen-specific cytotoxicity. IP10-modified CAR-T cells secreted IP10 upon antigen stimulation and demonstrated enhanced CXCR3-dependent chemotactic migration. In vivo , H9 CAR-IP10 T cells enhanced tumor growth inhibition, with 3 of 5 mice surviving by day 47 (including one tumor-free), whereas all controls died by day 41. Mechanistically, IP10 promoted early intratumoral T cell infiltration and, at later stages, reduced CLDN18.2 expression and increased CD31 expression, suggesting tumor vascular remodeling, though survival benefit did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.24). Dual IP10/IL-15 modification further enhanced antitumor activity, producing pronounced survival benefit with 3 of 5 mice tumor-free at day 78 and 90% reduction in mortality risk (p = 0.0069). Discussion In conclusion, our preclinical findings demonstrate IP10 modification enhances CLDN18.2 CAR-T cell efficacy by promoting T cell infiltration and remodeling the vascular microenvironment, and dual IP10/IL-15 modification yields potent and durable antitumor benefits at low doses, offering a promising strategy that warrants further validation in orthotopic and clinically relevant models.

works.title: Correction: Sialylation-Siglec glyco-immune checkpoints in hepatocellular carcinoma: mechanisms of immune evasion, therapeutic resistance, and postoperative recurrence
Medicinal plants in diabetic nephropathy: bioactive compounds, mechanisms, and therapeutic potential
works.abstract: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is known as one of the most critical microvascular complications associated with diabetes mellitus, and is a primary cause of chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease worldwide. Renal injury in DN is primarily driven by persistent hyperglycemia, which sequentially triggers oxidative stress, activation of innate immune signaling pathways, pro-inflammatory cytokine production, accumulation of advanced glycation end products, activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), and extracellular matrix deposition. Exisitng treatments, such as glycemic control, antihypertensive agents, and RAAS inhibitors, are efficacious in slowing disease progression. Alongside these standard therapies, medicinal plants and their bioactive constituents have garnered substantial attention as potential complementary approaches. The aim of this review is to highlight the therapeutic potential of medicinal plants and their phytoconstituents, leading to the prevention and management of DN, while elucidating associated pharmacological mechanisms. Several in vitro and in vivo studies have shown that various medicinal plants exert nephroprotective effects through antihyperglycemic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and lipid-lowering mechanisms, as well as by inactivating innate immune pathways. Notable phytoconstituents, including quercetin, rutin, curcumin, berberine, mangiferin, gallic acid, and thymoquinone, have demonstrated promising potential in enhancing renal biomarkers, reducing oxidative stress, suppressing inflammatory mediators, and preserving renal tissue structure. Altogether, medicinal plants emerge as promising multi-target therapeutic candidates for DN, warranting rigorous clinical trials to better evaluate their future therapeutic translation.

works.title: Navigating post-transplant relapse in acute myeloid leukemia: donor lymphocyte infusion, emerging cellular immunotherapies, and clinical management
works.abstract: Relapse after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) remains the major obstacle to curing acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Even with modern advances, it continues to be the leading cause of treatment failure. The biology behind post-transplant relapse is multifaceted: leukemic cells evolve ways to evade immune detection, donor immune cells can become dysfunctional, the bone marrow microenvironment shifts in ways that favor leukemia, and the transplant itself reshapes immune dynamics in complex ways. This review brings these pieces together by combining mechanistic understanding with practical, evidence-based treatment pathways. The goal is to offer a clear framework for both preventing relapse and managing it when it occurs. We also highlight emerging strategies—such as biomarker-guided interventions, more precise immune modulation, microbiome-based approaches, and the integration of patient-reported outcomes—that aim to improve long-term disease control and overall survivorship. Current tools for risk assessment and immune monitoring are summarized, including measurable residual disease (MRD), donor chimerism, TIM-3 + leukemic stem cell tracking, leukemia-associated antigen-specific T-cell responses, and microbiome profiling. Together, these approaches help clinicians better anticipate relapse, tailor interventions, and refine post-transplant care.

works.title: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor at the osteoimmune interface: from bone homeostasis to degenerative, metabolic, and inflammatory disorders
works.abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is a transcription factor activated by ligands, which participates in multiple environmental, microbial, and metabolic signals and plays a crucial role in maintaining homeostasis. In the past, AhR was regarded as a receptor for environmental toxins, several studies in recent years have indicated a potentially significant association between AhR and bone and joint health. This review systematically describes AhR signaling pathways (including canonical and non-canonical pathways) and its ligands, and focuses on the direct regulatory role of AhR in osteoblast and osteoclast function. Additionally, this review deeply explores the immunoregulatory role of AhR in T cells and macrophages, as well as how AhR-mediated interactions between immune cells and bone cells shape the bone immune microenvironment. In addition, this review systematically reviews the mechanisms of tryptophan metabolites as AhR ligands regulating bone metabolism through the gut-immune-bone axis, and comprehensively evaluates the pathological significance of AhR in bone and joint diseases such as osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Finally, this review explores AhR-targeted therapeutic strategies and the challenges they face, providing a new theoretical basis and viable research directions for the targeted treatment of bone and joint diseases.

works.title: An ecological framework linking intratumoral microbiota to antitumor immunity in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
works.abstract: Intratumoral bacteria have been linked to antitumor immunity, but the relevance of these findings to laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma remains uncertain. We propose a framework that integrates absolute bacterial load, spatial and cellular localization, and the surrounding immune state. The framework distinguishes an association that may support risk stratification from a causal mechanism requiring temporal and experimental evidence. We specify candidate decision rules for detection above background, quantitative load categories, cellular association, and neutrophil enrichment with CD8 T cell exclusion. These rules require prospective calibration and must be locked before independent validation. A ranked sampling strategy prioritizes tumor tissue, safely obtainable adjacent mucosa, and blood while allowing restricted analyses when compartments are missing. Paired sampling around planned checkpoint blockade can characterize immune changes over time but cannot establish microbial causality by itself. Selective bacterial depletion, matched add-back, and immune perturbation in appropriate laryngeal models are needed to test the proposed mechanism. This approach retains taxonomic information while making the load and localization hypothesis measurable, clinically feasible, and open to refutation. It does not support empirical antibiotic treatment or current treatment selection from unvalidated microbial states.

works.title: Peripheral T-helper 17 and regulatory T-cell frequencies in preeclampsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
works.abstract: Background Preeclampsia is associated with immune dysregulation, but reported alterations in circulating T helper 17 (Th17) and regulatory T (Treg) cells vary across studies. We systematically evaluated peripheral Th17 and Treg relative frequencies and the Th17/Treg ratio in women with preeclampsia. Methods PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception through September 15, 2026 for observational studies providing case–control comparisons of peripheral-blood Th17 or Treg frequencies between women with preeclampsia and healthy pregnant controls. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using inverse-variance random-effects models. Canonical phenotype definitions were used for the primary analyses, with broader phenotype definitions examined in sensitivity analyses. Results Twenty-two studies were included. In the strict primary analyses, women with preeclampsia had higher peripheral Th17 relative frequencies (12 datasets; SMD = 0.78, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.99; I² = 28%), lower Treg relative frequencies (10 datasets; SMD = -1.03, 95% CI -1.57 to -0.49; I² = 88%), and a higher Th17/Treg ratio (4 datasets; SMD = 1.23, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.68; I² = 54%). Broader-phenotype sensitivity analyses showed the same direction of association. Leave-one-out and alternative statistical-method sensitivity analyses did not materially change the direction of the pooled estimates. Conclusions Established preeclampsia is associated with higher circulating Th17 relative frequencies, lower Treg relative frequencies, and a higher Th17/Treg ratio. These findings support an association with altered peripheral immune-cell balance but do not establish causality, predictive utility, or T-cell functional impairment. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/ , identifier CRD42024606041.

works.title: Efficacy and safety of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based regimens for advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma: a Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
works.abstract: Background Direct head-to-head evidence comparing different immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based regimens for advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma remains limited. This study aimed to synthesize direct and indirect evidence to evaluate efficacy and safety of relevant immunotherapy regimens and to provide references for clinical practice. Methods Four electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science were searched up to July 2026. The primary endpoints were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR) and the incidence of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). The risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2.0 tool. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was performed, and surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values were calculated for treatment ranking. A prespecified subgroup analysis was conducted according to PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS). Results Ten randomized controlled trials involving 7, 728 patients were included. The primary analysis was restricted to the eight first-line RCTs (n = 6, 643) to satisfy the transitivity assumption. Compared with chemotherapy alone, ICI-containing regimens significantly improved OS (HR = 0.776, 95% CI 0.712-0.845, P < 0.0001), PFS (HR = 0.705, 95% CI 0.624-0.797, P < 0.0001), and ORR (OR = 1.598, 95% CI 1.394-1.832, P < 0.0001). A modest but statistically significant increase in grade ≥3 TRAEs was detected with ICI addition (OR = 1.143, 95% CI 1.026-1.274, P = 0.016). Survival benefits varied according to PD-L1 CPS; significant improvements were observed in patients with CPS ≥5 and CPS 1-4, whereas the benefit did not reach statistical significance in those with CPS <1. SUCRA ranking suggested that PD-1/CTLA-4 bispecific antibody plus chemotherapy had the highest probability of being the optimal OS strategy. Conclusions In patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, ICI-containing regimens significantly improved OS, PFS, and ORR over chemotherapy alone, with greater benefit at higher PD-L1 CPS and a modest but significant increase in grade ≥3 TRAEs that should be weighed against the survival benefit. Treatment rankings derived from indirect evidence carry considerable uncertainty and should not be interpreted as definitive superiority; confirmation in prospective head-to-head trials is warranted.

works.title: Correction: Targeting P2Y12 limits TH17 accumulation in the CNS and reduces EAE progression
Prognostic and diagnostic value of gelsolin in sepsis: a meta-analysis and systematic review
works.abstract: Background Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, leading to substantial morbidity and mortality. Reliable biomarkers that support early diagnosis and risk stratification are still in great need. Gelsolin (GSN), an actin-binding protein involved in cytoskeletal remodeling, actin scavenging, and inflammatory regulation, has been proposed as a potential biomarker in sepsis, but the available clinical evidence has not been systematically summarized. Methods PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library and clinical trial registries were searched from database inception to July 26, 2026. Original studies that measured circulating GSN levels in adult patients with sepsis and reported either survival outcomes or comparisons with a control group were eligible. The ratio of means (ROM) was used to compare GSN levels between non-survivors and survivors. For diagnostic analyses, sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratios (ORs), and post-test probabilities were summarized when sufficient data were available. Results Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. In seven studies reporting survival outcomes, GSN levels were significantly lower in non-survivors than in survivors (ROM = 0.62, 95% CI:0.53-0.73, P < 0.00001), with high statistical heterogeneity ( I 2 = 74%). One study reported an admission plasma GSN threshold of 113.6 mg/L that showed prognostic discrimination for 28-day mortality; however, this single study derived threshold should be considered exploratory because it requires external validation and may not be generalizable given variations in assay methods and reported cut-off values across studies. Three studies were included in the exploratory diagnostic analysis. The pooled sensitivity was 0.81 (95% CI:0.71-0.89), whereas specificity was modest at 0.61 (95% CI:0.49-0.72) with substantial heterogeneity across studies ( I 2 = 90.6%), indicating considerable variability in false-positive classification. The positive likelihood ratio was 2.19 and the diagnostic OR was 6.38; however, these estimates should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of studies, heterogeneous comparator groups, and variability in diagnostic settings. Conclusions Lower circulating GSN levels are associated with mortality in patients with sepsis and may have value for early prognostic risk stratification. However, because GSN is reduced in several inflammatory and tissue-injury conditions and because diagnostic specificity was modest with substantial heterogeneity, GSN should not be considered a stand-alone diagnostic biomarker for sepsis. Further larger multicenter prospective studies using standardized assays and clinically relevant comparator groups are needed to validate its prognostic and diagnostic utility. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/ , identifier CRD420261463914.

works.title: Beyond apoptosis: calpains as guardians of T-cell quiescence and self-tolerance – a systematic review
works.abstract: Calpains, a family of Ca² + -activated proteases classically studied in cell-death pathways, are emerging as regulators of immune quiescence and tolerance, and may contribute to immune activation thresholds through distinct substrates including ZAP-70, NF-κB, and Cyclin D1. A systematic literature search according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, which involved searching PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library for records between 1990 and September 2026, was performed, and a total of 281 articles were recorded. Out of the total, 125 studies met inclusion criteria and were thus included in the review after a thorough title/abstract and full-text assessment. Across the included studies, calpains emerged as potential regulators of lymphocyte quiescence by acting on cell-cycle progression and T-cell receptor signaling pathways through proteolytic cleavage of Cyclin D1, and c-Myc, respectively. In addition, proposed regulation of checkpoint molecules such as PD-1 and CTLA-4 implicated calpain activity in immune self-tolerance, although direct cleavage evidence remains limited. Calpain dysregulation may contribute to immune suppression when proteolysis is excessive or to autoimmune disease when proteolysis is insufficient. In fact, preclinical data showed that pharmacological inhibition of calpains reduced the severity of autoimmune disease and inflammation; however, human efficacy data for calpain inhibition in autoimmune disease have not been established. Calpain dysregulation, irrespective of whether there is an increase or decrease in proteolysis, seems to cause diverse types of immune disorders, from immunosuppression to autoimmunity. This means that targeting calpains might be a possible therapeutic approach in autoimmune disease, chronic infections, and cancer.

works.title: Eosinophils in cancer immunity: context-dependent plasticity, biomarker potential, and therapeutic opportunities
works.abstract: Eosinophils, traditionally associated with type 2 immunity, are increasingly recognized as context-dependent regulators of cancer immunity. Their effects are not intrinsically anti-tumorigenic or pro-tumorigenic but are shaped by five partially distinct dimensions of context: tumor type and stage, anatomical compartment and microlocalization, cytokine milieu and activation state, the circulating-versus-tissue compartment, and treatment exposure. This Review critically synthesizes mechanistic and clinical evidence defining this functional plasticity, with explicit separation of murine and human evidence throughout. Eosinophils can directly kill tumor cells through granule proteins and reactive oxygen species, recruit and activate cytotoxic lymphocytes, promote vascular normalization, and participate in interleukin-33-dependent anti-tumor circuits. In other settings, they can facilitate metastatic dissemination, angiogenesis, tissue remodeling, and immune suppression. These opposing functions help explain the heterogeneous clinical associations reported across malignancies. Tissue eosinophils at the invasive tumor front are associated with longer time to recurrence in colorectal cancer, whereas peripheral eosinophil dynamics have emerged as candidate biomarkers during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in non-small cell lung cancer; eosinophilic malignant pleural effusion may also define a distinct prognostic subgroup. We critically distinguish prognostic, predictive, and pharmacodynamic biomarker claims, and emphasize that most reported associations remain prognostic rather than demonstrated predictors of treatment benefit. We further discuss therapeutic opportunities involving the interleukin-5/interleukin-33/eotaxin axis, induced eosinophils, and eosinophil-assisted cellular therapy, graded by their level of clinical maturity and weighed against the risks of systemic eosinophil activation. We argue that clinically useful eosinophil biomarkers will require integration of abundance with phenotype, spatial localization, tissue compartment, and treatment context. This framework clarifies when eosinophils are protective, harmful, or therapeutically exploitable and highlights priorities for prospective human studies in cancer immunology and precision immunotherapy.

works.title: Application and future prospects of bispecific antibodies in the treatment of colorectal cancer
works.abstract: Over the past decade, the incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) has continued to rise, imposing a substantial disease burden on both patients and society. Improvements in treatment strategies—including surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy—have significantly improved clinical outcomes. Immunotherapy, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors, has shown promising efficacy in rectal cancer studies. Nevertheless, multiple CRC subtypes are still hindered by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, the development of therapeutic resistance, and low response rates to immunotherapy, collectively limiting further gains in clinical benefit. As an emerging therapeutic modality, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) possess two binding specificities, enabling them to bind simultaneously to the same or different antigens, thereby generating multifaceted anti-tumor effects. Therefore, BsAbs can help overcome treatment resistance and potentiate antitumor immune responses. To date, numerous BsAbs have been used in clinical trials to assess their safety and efficacy across diverse CRC subtypes. This review summarizes the main classes of BsAbs used for CRC treatment, focusing on their mechanisms of action and recent advances in clinical research. We further discuss existing challenges for BsAbs and the potential strategies.

works.title: A PiggyBac-based PSR vector system for construction of stable self-inactivating γ-retrovirus producer cell lines
works.abstract: Introduction γ-retroviral vectors (RVs) are broadly applied in cell therapy, yet self-inactivating γ-retroviral vectors (SIN-RVs), which possess superior biosafety, are conventionally produced via transient transfection and face major barriers for large-scale manufacturing. Here, we established a PiggyBac transposon-based platform, termed PSR, to generate stable SIN-RV producer cells. Methods The PSR platform was constructed using the pSRS11.SF.GFP backbone. CopGFP reporter and puromycin resistance markers were integrated to simplify screening of stable producer cell populations. These markers are exclusively expressed in the vector producer cell lines rather than in transduced target cells, and are not packaged into SIN-RV particles, representing a favorable safety feature. The SFFV promoter was used as the internal promoter, and the U3 region within the 5′-LTR was replaced with an RSV chimeric promoter. PSR.EGFP was packaged to characterize vector production, and SIN-RV encoding SynCAR190 was further generated as an application example. Results and conclusion Viral supernatant of PSR.EGFP derived from Phoenix-Ampho cells reached a titer of 1.6 × 10 7 TU/mL, which is >100-fold higher than the 1.3 × 10 5 TU/mL from PG13 cells, supporting Phoenix-Ampho as a highly suitable packaging cell line under our experimental conditions. With polybrene treatment, one round of transduction using PSR.EGFP supernatant achieved 70.2% transduction efficiency in Jurkat-T cells (MOI = 10). Among 15 monoclonal PSR.SynCAR190 clones, clone A190–5 was selected for characterization. This clone produced viral supernatant with a titer of 2.39 × 10 6 TU/mL and yielded a 56.27% transduction efficiency in primary T cells (MOI = 6), with the observed titer reduction consistent with the large transgene insert size. In vitro assays indicated that SynCAR190-T cells preferentially targeted CD19 + BCMA + double-positive tumor cells while exhibiting minimal cytotoxicity against single-positive cells. These preliminary functional validations are consistent with the intended gating design. Collectively, this engineered PSR platform provides a feasible approach for generating stable SIN-RV producer cells at laboratory scale.

works.title: Temporal misalignment in rheumatoid arthritis: a model linking microbial metabolic rhythms, circadian clocks, and inflammatory timing
works.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) exhibits pronounced time-of-day variation in inflammatory activity, including nocturnal cytokine elevation and early-morning symptom exacerbation. Although circadian disruption, gut microbial alterations, and immune dysregulation have each been implicated in RA, these processes have largely been studied as temporally independent phenomena. Here, we propose the temporal misalignment model, which reframes RA inflammatory timing as a disturbance in the relative timing among gut microbial metabolic rhythms, host circadian clocks, and immune effector processes. The model distinguishes three measurable dimensions of temporal organisation: inter-system phase relationships, oscillatory amplitude relevant to temporal coupling, and cross-system coherence. Microbiota-associated metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan-related metabolites, and bile acids are proposed as candidate mediators because they exhibit time-of-day variation and can modulate host clock-related pathways, although direct evidence for such coupling in human RA remains limited. The model predicts that cross-system temporal abnormalities may precede clinically apparent RA, contribute to heterogeneity in chronotherapy response, and propagate downstream when microbial rhythmicity is experimentally perturbed. Crucially, restoration of microbial rhythmicity without corresponding realignment of host clock, immune, and inflammatory timing would challenge the proposed causal framework. By treating temporal relationships as measurable biological variables, the temporal misalignment model extends existing neuroendocrine and gut–joint frameworks and provides a falsifiable basis for time-resolved mechanistic studies in RA.

works.title: Disordered lymphatic function in human primary lymphatic anomalies is associated with shortened circulating memory CD4+ T-cell lifespans
works.abstract: Primary lymphatic anomalies (PLA) are disorders characterised by interstitial accumulation of lymph due to dysfunctional lymphatics. T cell lymphopenia occurs in these anomalies irrespective of cause, primarily affecting less-differentiated CD4+ populations. The mechanism is unknown although counts are lower when central lymphatics are involved (‘systemic disease’). We tested whether such lymphopenia is likely to result from reduced T-cell survival by labelling dividing cells in vivo using deuterium-labelled glucose. 15 PLA patients (6 ‘simplex’ with no internal involvement, 9 systemic) and 8 healthy controls received 6,6- 2 H 2 -glucose. Over the ensuing 21 days, we separated blood CD4 + T-cell subsets: naïve (TN); central memory (TCM); transitional memory (TTM). Deuterium incorporation into DNA was measured as a marker of cell division. Results were compared to CD4 counts alongside immunophenotyping for activation (HLA-DR/CD38), proliferation (Ki67) and apoptosis (Annexin V). CD4 depletion was associated with both reduced memory and naïve cell numbers, In circulating TCM, more cells were labelled (recently divided) in PLA than controls (p=0.017) suggesting either accelerated proliferation and/or reduced lifespans. There was a correlation between CD4 depletion and reduced lifespan for both TCM and TTM (p=0.011 and 0.019 respectively) indicative of shorter memory cell lifespans in those most lymphopenic. Labelling in TN cells was largely undetectable, consistent with slow turnover, but TN activation and Ki67 expression were increased in systemic PLA subjects. Reduced T-cell survival appears to be an important contributor to lymphopenia in PLA, demonstrating the pivotal role of lymphatic function in lymphocyte homeostasis.

works.title: Left ventricular thrombus following axitinib plus toripalimab therapy in metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma: a case report
works.abstract: Background The combination of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (VEGFR-TKIs) and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitors has become a standard first-line treatment for advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). However, cardiovascular toxicities associated with this combination require further clinical attention. Here, we report a rare case of left ventricular (LV) thrombus occurring following axitinib plus toripalimab therapy in metastatic ccRCC and discuss its clinical management strategy. Case presentation A 60-year-old woman with stage IV ccRCC (cT2aN1M1) and bilateral pulmonary metastases achieved a partial response after two cycles of axitinib (5 mg twice daily) combined with toripalimab (240 mg every 21 days). After two cycles at month 1.5, Grade 3 immune-related hepatitis developed, requiring discontinuation of both toripalimab and axitinib, followed by prolonged corticosteroid therapy. After four weeks of corticosteroid treatment, liver transaminases improved, prompting the resumption of axitinib monotherapy while corticosteroids were completely tapered off over a total course of five weeks. Three months after starting initial combination therapy, corresponding to approximately two weeks after axitinib resumption, the patient presented with exertional fatigue. Echocardiography revealed a heterogeneous hyperechoic mass in the mid-anterior wall of the left ventricle with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (46%). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) further confirmed the presence of an LV thrombus. Axitinib was discontinued, and anticoagulation therapy with nadroparin calcium followed by warfarin was initiated. Complete thrombus resolution was achieved after three months; however, prolonged interruption of antineoplastic therapy was followed by disease progression. Conclusion This case highlights LV thrombus as a complex, multifactorial cardiovascular event occurring during the course of VEGFR-TKI and ICI therapy in advanced ccRCC. Careful cardiovascular monitoring and multidisciplinary management are essential for early recognition and individualized treatment of this potentially serious complication.

works.title: Lipid droplets as the metabolic switch of macrophage resolution
works.abstract: Macrophages play a key role in cellular immunity and metabolism, and their lipid handling is a crucial determinant of whether inflammation resolves or becomes chronic. Lipid droplets (LDs) are now recognized as active organelles that regulate free cholesterol and fatty acids and influence immune signaling. This review examines the reciprocal relationship between LDs and efferocytosis, the clearance of apoptotic cells. Successful efferocytosis promotes cholesterol efflux and pro-resolving signaling, thereby reinforcing the capacity for subsequent clearance. Conversely, pro-inflammatory macrophages accumulate LDs; disrupted lipid balance impairs efferocytosis at multiple stages. We propose that LD coat proteins and lipases regulate droplet turnover and, consequently, macrophage engulfment capacity. We further suggest that this principle extends beyond efferocytosis, as LD turnover may supply lipid and membrane components that support the membrane remodeling and cytoskeletal processes required for large-particle engulfment. Importantly, this switch is bidirectional and context-dependent rather than a simple rule that lipid-droplet accumulation is harmful: whether droplet build-up is adaptive or maladaptive depends on inflammatory phase, polarization state, and tissue niche. Together, these observations position the LD enzyme and coat protein machinery as potential regulators of macrophage engulfment capacity.

works.title: Nanomatrix-based TCR stimulation supports CD4+ but not CD8+ T cell effector functions
works.abstract: Introduction In vitro T cell stimulation is commonly used to model physiological TCR-pMHC engagement to study T cell activation, signaling, proliferation, and differentiation. Classical stimulation methods use anti-CD3 antibodies combined with anti-CD28 antibodies, in soluble or plate-bound forms. This promotes TCR crosslinking and robust activation. Here, we evaluated TransAct, a soluble nanomatrix-conjugated antibody reagent, as an alternative to conventional antibody-based stimulation methods. Methods Both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies or TransAct, and proliferation, cytokine production, and the expression of activation markers were assessed by flow cytometry. Additionally, TCR polarization was analyzed by ImageStream analysis. Results Whereas T cell proliferation was comparable for CD4 + T cells stimulated with TransAct or anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies, it was dramatically reduced in TransAct-stimulated CD8 + T cells compared to the antibody treatment. Stimulation with antibodies elicited high levels of IL-2, IFN, and TNF in both subsets, whereas TransAct generally triggered lower cytokine production, with particularly attenuated responses in CD8 + T cells. The early activation markers CD69 and CD25 were upregulated by TransAct in CD4 + T cells and, to a lesser extent, in CD8 + T cells. However, the late activation marker HLA-DR, activation-associated inhibitory receptors (PD-1, CTLA-4), and FoxP3 were more strongly induced by antibodies, particularly in CD8 + T cells. Imaging flow cytometry analysis confirmed altered spatial organization of the TCR complex after TransAct stimulation compared to antibody stimulation. Discussion These findings indicate that TransAct provides effective, relatively gentle activation of CD4 + T cells but delivers suboptimal activation signals to CD8 + T cells compared to classical plate-bound antibody stimulation.

works.title: Multi-cohort and single-cell multi-omic analyses reveal multicellular mechanotransduction–immune remodeling in rheumatoid arthritis synovium
works.abstract: Background Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovitis integrates immune-cell recruitment, stromal remodeling and persistent inflammation, but its relationship with tissue mechanotransduction remains unclear. We investigated whether RA involves coordinated remodeling of multicellular mechanotransduction–immune programs. Methods We constructed a 327-gene mechanotransduction compendium and used GSE89408 synovial transcriptomes from healthy controls (n = 28), patients with osteoarthritis (n = 22) and patients with RA (n = 152) for discovery. Candidates prioritized through RA-versus-Healthy and RA-versus-OA contrasts were evaluated in three patient-independent cohorts using validation-only random-effects meta-analysis. Co-expression networks, consensus clustering, locked external mapping, single-cell RNA sequencing, cell–cell communication inference, virtual knockout and single-cell chromatin-accessibility analyses (11 RA donors and one OA reference; no healthy controls) resolved network, cellular and regulatory contexts. Selected gene-expression findings were examined by quantitative PCR in independent healthy (n = 20) and RA (n = 25) synovial tissues and by overexpression and siRNA-mediated knockdown in synovial fibroblasts. Results In unadjusted bulk-tissue profiles, RA synovium showed higher expression-based scores for integrin–extracellular matrix sensing and nuclear LINC programs but lower scores for focal-adhesion force-transmission and Hippo–YAP/TAZ-associated genes. Composition adjustment attenuated several of these associations. Nine candidates met the prespecified meta-analysis criteria and mapped to four co-expression modules associated with adaptive and innate immune programs, cell cycling and mechanotransduction-related expression scores. Tissue qPCR reproduced the predicted expression directions. Two molecular states with distinct inflammatory and mechanotransduction-associated expression features were recovered in external cohorts. In exploratory analyses, TLN2 and NRXN1 expression was inversely associated with inflammatory mediators and DAS28. Exploratory single-cell analyses localized the programs to fibroblast, myeloid, lymphoid and proliferating states and inferred differences in fibroblast–myeloid communication potential. Perturbing TLN2 or NRXN1 altered selected ECM-associated transcripts and COL1A1 protein, with corresponding changes in Matrigel invasion within one donor, while transcription-factor perturbation supported candidate FOXP2–NRXN1, NFIX–NRXN1/TLN2 and FOS–TLN2 expression relationships. Conclusions Patient-derived multi-omic and experimental evidence supports coordinated transcriptional remodeling of a multicellular mechanotransduction–immune network associated with RA synovial heterogeneity.

works.title: Extracellular vesicles in osteoarthritis: mechanisms, biomarkers and translational strategies
works.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint disorder characterized by cartilage degeneration, synovial inflammation, subchondral bone remodeling, pain and progressive functional impairment. Current management remains largely symptomatic, and no widely accepted disease-modifying therapy is available. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate intercellular communication by transferring regulatory RNAs, proteins, lipids, metabolites and other bioactive molecules. Their effects depend on the source and state of the donor cell, cargo composition, recipient phenotype, dose and disease context. EVs released by inflamed or mechanically stressed joint tissues can amplify matrix catabolism, inflammasome activation, senescence, defective autophagy and osteochondral crosstalk. By contrast, selected mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived, preconditioned, engineered or biomaterial-delivered EV preparations show reparative and immunomodulatory activity in preclinical models. Synovial-fluid and circulating EV profiles are also being investigated as biomarkers, although independent validation remains limited. In this narrative review, we integrate EV-mediated communication across cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone and immune compartments. We also critically assess the evidence for OA biomarkers and cell-free therapies. Current evidence supports EVs as candidate biomarkers and experimental therapeutic platforms, but does not yet establish their clinical diagnostic utility or therapeutic efficacy in OA. Translation requires independent biomarker validation, standardized EV characterization and dosing, mechanism-linked potency assays, and controlled clinical trials that distinguish symptomatic improvement from structural disease modification.

works.title: Immune-stromal-lymphatic communication shapes the context-dependent relationship between Hashimoto thyroiditis and papillary thyroid carcinoma
works.abstract: Hashimoto thyroiditis (HT) and papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) frequently coexist, yet their clinical relationship remains paradoxical. Surgical and epidemiological series establish heterogeneous clinical associations: PTC is detected more often in some HT cohorts, whereas coexistent HT is associated with less aggressive disease in many outcome studies. Tissue studies separately establish organized autoimmune inflammation in HT and heterogeneous immune, stromal, endothelial, and lymphatic programs in PTC. What is not established is that these compartments form a single causal mechanism at the HT-PTC interface. The principal contribution of this review is therefore a hypothesis-generating, spatially explicit framework asking whether autoimmune tissue architecture that may predate tumor detection modifies subsequent tumor evolution. We distinguish distant autoimmune follicles from tumor-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs), and we separate direct HT-PTC observations from HT-only evidence, PTC evidence that is not HT-specific, and mechanistic extrapolation. The proposed framework integrates CCL21-CCR7 and CXCL13-CXCR5 signaling, ACKR1-positive endothelial entry sites, fibroblast states, TLS phenotype and location, and VEGF-C/VEGF-D-VEGFR3-associated lymphatic remodeling. These processes may have different relevance to tumor initiation and to progression after PTC is established. Depending on region, tumor genotype, immune function, stromal state, and tumor-lymphatic proximity, an inflamed gland may support epithelial injury, productive antitumor immunity, an inflamed but ineffective immune state, or lymphatic dissemination. These spatial features remain mechanistic and exploratory prognostic candidates; they are not validated diagnostic, predictive, or treatment-directing biomarkers. Region-matched human studies, functional perturbation, independent retrospective validation, and prospective clinical-utility testing are required.

works.title: Mechanometabolic regulation of CAR-NK cells in solid tumors: evidence, engineering hypotheses, and translational constraints
works.abstract: CAR-NK cells offer an allogeneic and potentially safer platform for adoptive cell therapy, yet their activity in solid tumors remains inconsistent and often limited by poor trafficking, short persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and suppressive tumor microenvironments. This narrative Review examines an underintegrated dimension of CAR-NK failure: the interaction between metabolic stress and mechanical constraints within solid tumors. We integrate evidence from NK/CAR-NK studies, related T-cell systems, and tumor mechanobiology across three axes: mitochondrial adaptation to hypoxia, lipid handling under nutrient stress, and responses to mechanically restrictive tumor environments. Hypoxia-associated mitochondrial fragmentation has mechanistic support in NK cells, with emerging evidence that DRP1 disruption preserves CAR-NK cytotoxicity under hypoxia. Lipid-associated NK-cell dysfunction is supported across several disease contexts, whereas CPT1A overexpression, SOAT1 inhibition, and GPX4/FSP1 augmentation remain candidate CAR-NK strategies. PIEZO1-dependent NK-cell mechanosensing is experimentally supported, but its proposed coupling to YAP/TAZ-mediated metabolic dysfunction requires direct validation. We propose that future CAR-NK design should combine antigen recognition with context-restricted metabolic and mechanobiological support, including inducible circuits, cytokine armoring, checkpoint editing, and standardized iPSC-derived and donor-derived allogeneic platforms. We distinguish interventions supported by direct preclinical CAR-NK evidence from candidate designs requiring validation, and identify the functional, safety, and manufacturing requirements for further translation.

works.title: IL-8 in Human Glioblastoma Tumors Instructs Immunosuppressive Myeloid Cells
works.abstract: Adult glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor that has yet to benefit from advances in immunotherapy. Prior studies report contrasting leukocyte immunophenotypes between tumors and an association between myeloid macrophage infiltration and worse patient outcomes. IL-8, a cytokine with both inflammatory and suppressive roles, was recently associated with M2 macrophage phenotypes in GBM. These observations raise key questions: do GBM macrophages suppress or support other immune cells, is IL-8 in GBM a mechanistic driver of GBM macrophage function, and can IL-8 instruct macrophages in situ within tumors? Here, functional experiments with primary human GBM tumor cells from initial surgical resections showed that IL-8 from GBM contributes to and is sufficient to instruct monocyte-derived macrophages that suppress healthy T cells. Notably, IL-8 protein expression was enriched in aggressive tumors contacting the V-SVZ region and was not associated with increased infiltration of cells expressing the IL-8 receptors CXCR1/CXCR2. Suppressor cells instructed by GBM ex vivo phenotypically matched myeloid macrophages observed in vivo, and neutralizing IL-8 during instruction blocked this and restored T cell proliferation. Analysis of IL-8 RNA showed the cytokine is primarily produced by CD45- tumor cells. These results suggest a model where ongoing IL-8 production by GBM cells maintains an immunosuppressive microenvironment by signaling to myeloid macrophages within the tumor. Immunotherapies relying on T cells should now investigate whether IL-8 blockade prevents instruction of macrophages into tumor-protective suppressor cells.

works.title: MicroRNA core machinery maintains mitochondrial integrity to empower cancer escape from natural killer cell cytotoxicity
works.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells offer a promising off-the-shelf platform for cancer immunotherapy, yet their clinical efficacy is often limited by tumor-intrinsic resistance. Here, we show that loss of core microRNA (miRNA) machinery components, Argonaute‑2 (AGO2) or Ankyrin Repeat Domain 52 (ANKRD52), renders tumor cells hypersensitive to NK cell-mediated killing in both co-culture and xenograft models. Mechanistically, genetic ablation of Ago2 or Ankrd52 impairs miRNA-mediated silencing of critical mitochondrial apoptotic regulators and NK-cell-associated ligands in tumor cells, exemplified by the disrupted repression of pro-apoptotic Bim transcripts by miR-24 and miR-29b, thereby unleashing rapid TNF-α-driven apoptosis. Additionally, metabolic and ultrastructural analyses demonstrate collapsed membrane potential, diminished ATP levels, and fragmented mitochondria in Ago2- or Ankrd52-mutant tumor cells, accompanied by a lower apoptotic threshold upon TNF-α or NK cell challenge. Genome‑wide CRISPR library screen further revealed a selective fitness dependency on mitochondrial electron‑transport and ATP‑synthase genes in mutant tumor cells. Collectively, these findings define defective miRNA machinery as a tumor‑intrinsic vulnerability that couples mitochondrial fragility with increased NK-mediated cytotoxicity, nominate miRNA‑pathway status as a predictive biomarker, and propose that co‑targeting mitochondrial metabolism or apoptosis may potentiate NK‑cell therapies.

works.title: l-carnitine links red meat consumption to inflammation
PKA signaling controls ILC3 homeostasis and IL-23-mediated inflammation in the gut
Dectin-2-dependent adaptive immunity governs intestinal clearance of systemic Candida albicans
works.abstract: Effective immunity to Candida albicans requires coordination between innate recognition and induction of adaptive CD4 T cell responses. While the C-type lectin receptor Clec4n (Dectin-2) is known to drive Th17 polarization, its role in shaping tissue-specific adaptive responses remains incompletely understood. Here, we used an OT-II antigen-specific CD4 T cell transfer model combined with OVA-expressing Candida albicans to dissect the function of Dectin-2 during systemic infection. We found that Dectin-2 is dispensable for antigen presentation and CD4 T cell priming in gut-draining lymph nodes. Moreover, we show that Dectin-2-deficient mice fail to control fungal growth in the intestinal mucosa, despite elevated local production of IL-17A and GM-CSF. The increased susceptibility of the Dectin-2-deficient mice was associated with impaired neutrophil activation in the intestinal mucosa. These findings identify a tissue-specific requirement for Dectin-2, linking local adaptive Th17 cytokine responses to granulocyte function, and revealing a previously unappreciated mechanism required for anti-fungal immune regulation at intestinal mucosal surface.

works.title: Combining a massively parallel reporter assay and human data to elucidate genetic mechanisms driving risk for juvenile idiopathic arthritis
works.abstract: Background While progress has been made in identifying the true risk-driving single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPS) on juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) risk haplotypes, the affected cells and target genes largely remain unknown. Methods We used data from a previously published massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) to query human data in the Database of Immune Cell eQTLs (DICE) and the Gene-Tissue Expression (GTEx) database to identify affected cells and target genes of MPRA-identified SNPs in immune cells and relevant tissues. Results SNPs identified on MPRA were associated with gene expression levels in a broad range of immune cells in the DICE database, including CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes, monocytes, NK cells, and B cells. MPRA-identified SNPs showed strong associations with gene expression in GTEx whole blood, spleen, and/or EBV-transformed lymphocytes. Conclusions Our data show the efficacy of combining MPRA and using human cells/tissue expression data to elucidate complex mechanisms driving genetic risk for JIA.
