works.title: Integrative functional-genomics analysis identifies CCT3 as a prognostic biomarker in osteosarcoma, involving the beta-catenin/c-MYC axis in malignant progression
works.abstract: Objective Osteosarcoma prognosis remains challenging, and reliable molecular determinants are lacking. We integrated multi-dimensional functional genomic and transcriptomic data to construct a prognostic model and investigated the key candidate gene CCT3 in osteosarcoma malignancy. Methods We intersected CRISPR-Cas9 dependency genes with differentially expressed genes to derive a 64-gene candidate pool, followed by stepwise Cox regression to build a risk model. Model performance was validated in training and external cohorts. Immune microenvironment, drug sensitivity, and experimental validation were performed following CCT3 knockdown. Results An 8-gene risk model was constructed and significantly stratified overall survival. The high-risk group showed lower immune scores, reduced immune-cell infiltration, and downregulation of multiple immune checkpoint genes, indicating an immune-poor phenotype. Among 7 drugs with differential sensitivity, the high-risk group was more sensitive to 6 agents, including AZ6102, while showing resistance to Entospletinib. CCT3 was overexpressed in osteosarcoma tissues and cell lines; its knockdown suppressed proliferation and clonogenicity. Mechanistically, CCT3 depletion attenuated Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and reduced stemness markers CD24 and c-MYC. Conclusion Our integrative approach establishes an effective prognostic model for osteosarcoma and identifies CCT3 as a pro-tumorigenic gene, likely through the beta-catenin/c-MYC axis, representing a promising prognostic biomarker and therapeutic vulnerability.

works.title: A bioengineered CATH-2 (1–15)-Ta1 (1–9) hybrid peptide attenuates LPS-induced inflammation and oxidative stress through LPS neutralization and TLR4/MD-2 modulation
works.abstract: Excessive activation of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-mediated Toll-like receptor 4/myeloid differentiation factor 2 (TLR4/MD-2) signaling pathway plays a central role in the pathogenesis of sepsis and other inflammatory disorders by promoting oxidative stress and uncontrolled cytokine production. In the present study, a novel CATH-Ta1 hybrid peptide (CTHP), was rationally designed by combining the endotoxin-binding domain of chicken cathelicidin-2 (CATH-2, 1–15) with the immunomodulatory fragment of Thymosin alpha-1 (Ta1, 1–9). The objective was to develop a multifunctional peptide with enhanced anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and endotoxin-neutralizing activities. Structural characterization showed that CTHP adopted an amphipathic α-helical conformation with favorable hydrophobicity and strong cationic character. Reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry confirmed successful synthesis of the peptide with > 98.5% purity and a molecular mass consistent with the theoretical value (~3148.7 Da). Functionally, CTHP exhibited significantly greater LPS-neutralizing activity than its parental peptides, achieving approximately 90% endotoxin neutralization at 50 μg/mL (p< 0.05). Furthermore, CTHP displayed minimal hemolytic activity (<15%) and significantly reduced lactate dehydrogenase release in RAW 264.7 macrophages, indicating superior biocompatibility and cytoprotective properties. Ex vivo pharmacokinetic analysis revealed a prolonged plasma half-life (85–90 min) compared with CATH-2 and Ta1, demonstrating enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation. In vivo , CTHP markedly attenuated LPS-induced liver injury by reducing serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and histopathological damage. Additionally, CTHP significantly suppressed serum TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β production (p<0.01) and effectively reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species accumulation in LPS-stimulated macrophages. Molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance analyses demonstrated that CTHP interacts with the TLR4/MD-2 complex, while Western blot analysis showed attenuation of LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, while western blot analysis confirmed inhibition of p-IKKβ, p-IκBα, and NF-κB p65 activation. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that CTHP effectively neutralizes LPS, suppresses oxidative stress, and attenuates LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, potentially involving interaction with the TLR4/MD-2 complex, thereby attenuating inflammatory responses both in vitro and in vivo . These findings highlight the protective potential of CTHP against LPS-induced endotoxemia and support further investigation of its therapeutic efficacy in endotoxin-mediated inflammatory disorders.

works.title: Immunogenicity and safety of inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine (CoronaVac) using a two-dose primary protocol in children and adolescents (Immunita-002, Brazil): a phase IV one-year follow-up
authors: Jordana Grazziela Alves Coelho dos Reis
works.abstract: Long-term evidence on the durability and quality of immune responses induced by the inactivated whole-virus CoronaVac vaccine in children and adolescents remains limited. We evaluated humoral and cellular immunity and safety over 12 months after completion of the primary vaccination schedule. In this phase IV longitudinal study, 640 children and adolescents aged 3–17 years who received two doses of CoronaVac were followed for 12 months. Humoral immunity was assessed by anti-Spike (anti-S) and anti-Nucleocapsid (anti-N) IgG ELISAs and neutralizing antibody assays against the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 B.1 lineage and Omicron BA.1 and BA.5 subvariants. Cellular immunity was evaluated through antigen-specific stimulation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells, multiplex quantification of soluble immune mediators, and immune network analysis. Safety and suspected COVID-19 cases were monitored throughout follow-up. Anti-S and anti-N IgG seropositivity remained high throughout follow-up (90-96% and 93-98%, respectively). Neutralizing antibodies against the ancestral B.1 lineage remained high in both age groups, although seropositivity decreased to 80% at 12 months among children aged 3–11 years. In contrast, cross-neutralization against Omicron BA.5 increased over time, reaching 100% seropositivity in both age groups at 12 months. Vaccination was associated with changes in chemokines, inflammatory and regulatory cytokines, and growth factors, alongside dynamic immune network remodeling. Antigen-specific PBMC stimulation demonstrated cytokine and chemokine responses one year after vaccination, with distinct profiles following ancestral and Omicron Spike stimulation. No additional adverse events were reported during the final six months. Previously reported serious adverse events resolved without vaccine-related sequelae, and no clinically reported COVID-19 cases occurred during the final six months of surveillance. CoronaVac induced persistent humoral responses and was associated with longitudinal changes in antigen-stimulated immune activity over 12 months. Integrated immunological analyses provide insights into the durability and coordination of immune responses following primary vaccination in children and adolescents, while the mechanisms underlying immune memory and the relationship between immune responses and clinical protection remain to be elucidated.

works.title: Single-cell immunology of autoimmune encephalitis: from antibody-defined syndromes to compartmentalized immune responses
works.abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis is diagnosed by the clinical syndrome and the presence of antibodies against neuronal surface or intracellular antigens, yet patients who share an antibody differ widely in severity, treatment response, and outcome. Antibody titre explains only part of this variation, because it does not describe the cells that produce the antibody, where they reside, or which other effectors are engaged. Single-cell RNA sequencing, paired single-cell B-cell and T-cell receptor sequencing, and single-cell multi-omics now allow these questions to be addressed directly in blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain tissue. We review evidence generated by these methods across antigen-defined autoimmune encephalitis. Anti-NMDAR studies describe B-cell expansion alongside compartment-specific T-cell states. In LGI1-antibody and CASPR2-antibody encephalitis, antigen-reactive B cells are enriched in cerebrospinal fluid, with evidence consistent with prior peripheral maturation and accompanying T-cell alterations. Ri- and GAD65-associated syndromes show distinct neuron-reactive or stem-cell-like memory T-cell populations, while antigen-reactive B cells may coexist. The review also considers compartment-specific responses, clonal maturation, change during treatment, and the practical constraints on clinical use. Most cohorts remain small, single-centre, and cross-sectional, and few findings have been validated prospectively. Single-cell immunology currently refines mechanistic understanding rather than replacing antibody-based diagnosis, and its near-term value lies in selecting candidates for functional testing and in defining variables for future trials.

works.title: Cell-type-divergent redox injury in rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus/lupus nephritis: evidence for ferroptosis-related remodeling and immune amplification
works.abstract: Persistent immune activation alone does not adequately explain the relationship between chronic inflammation, structural damage, and incomplete tissue recovery in rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus/lupus nephritis. This review uses a cell-type-divergent redox-injury framework to organize how redox imbalance is translated into distinct cellular outcomes. The framework links disruption of SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 antioxidant defenses to lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative modification of self-molecules, damage-associated molecular pattern release, and neutrophil extracellular trap–immune complex–type I interferon amplification. Its central premise is that similar inflammatory redox pressure may promote the loss or dysfunction of tissue-supporting or inflammation-resolving cells, permit pathogenic proliferative cells to persist through reinforced anti-ferroptotic defenses, and sustain post-injury immune amplification. Rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus/lupus nephritis provide the most developed disease-specific evidence and therefore form the primary focus of this review, whereas evidence in other rheumatic diseases remains heterogeneous and is often indirect, transcriptomic, or model-dependent. Even within RA and SLE/LN, however, the maturity of cell-specific mechanistic evidence is uneven: the macrophage HMGB1–TLR4–STAT3 amplification circuit has been demonstrated in a single mechanistic RA study, whereas individual upstream regulators of podocyte ferroptosis-like injury in LN remain incompletely replicated and predominantly supported by preclinical evidence. Within this framework, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and pyroptosis should not be regarded as interchangeable processes. The framework supports a cell-directed therapeutic logic centered on protecting vulnerable structural cells and selected inflammation-resolving immune-cell states, selectively restoring ferroptotic susceptibility in pathogenic proliferative cells, and interrupting downstream inflammatory amplification while avoiding indiscriminate antioxidant or tissue-wide ferroptosis modulation.

works.title: Tumour immune ecosystem in bone tumours: resolving the bone-tumour paradox from spatial architecture to systemic remodelling
works.abstract: Malignant bone tumours, encompassing osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and bone metastases secondary to solid tumours, remain among the malignancies with the poorest clinical prognoses. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors have significantly altered the therapeutic landscape across multiple solid tumours, objective response rates in bone tumours have consistently remained extremely low. This striking discordance—wherein the physiologically immune-rich bone marrow niche manifests as a pathological “cold tumour” phenotype—defines the “bone tumour paradox” and highlights the inherent limitations of conventional tumour microenvironment theory in the bone-specific context. Drawing on recent advances in spatial multi-omics, mechanobiology, and immunology, this review proposes the Tumour Immune Ecosystem (TIE) framework, which conceptualises the bone-tumour microenvironment as a highly self-organising, evolutionarily resilient pathological ecosystem. It delineates the spatial architecture comprising the Mechanical Impedance Zone (MIZ) and Immune Exclusion Zone (IEZ), dissects the fivefold defensive barriers—physical impedance, recognition decoupling, niche occupancy, metabolic constraints, and molecular locking—and their non-linear coupling mechanisms that sustain systemic immune resistance. Building upon this framework, the review proposes the Ablation–Normalisation–Priming (ANP) three-stage sequential ecosystem remodelling strategy as a conceptual, hypothesis-driven pathway to systematically dismantle these multidimensional barriers. The TIE framework and ANP strategy provide a novel integrative perspective for resolving the bone-tumour paradox, offering critical insights into cold-tumour microenvironments and embodying a paradigm shift from component-based interventions toward multidimensional systemic ecosystem governance in bone tumour immunotherapy. As a conceptual strategy synthesising primarily preclinical and non-bone-tumour-specific evidence, further experimental and clinical validation will be required.

works.title: Editorial: Community series in novel reliable approaches for prediction and clinical decision-making in cancer, volume II
works.abstract: immunotherapeutic approaches in patients who are resistant to established immunotherapies. Based on public expression profile data, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) two distinct patterns of disulfidptosis genes are identified as an independent prognostic factor for overall survival by consensus cluster analysis (Zhang X. et al., 2025). The combination of single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data shows that the two expression patterns differ regarding immune cell infiltration and signaling pathways. Data on immunotherapy provide evidence of predictive potential for response of immunotherapy. As part of a drug screening, AZD8186 and JQ1 are identified as potential treatment options for patients with a less favorable prognostic disulfidptosis signature, introducing a new theoretical basis for clinical decision-making. In lung adenocarcinoma (Zhang Y. et al., 2024), two distinct cancer subtypes (CSs) are identified as independent predictors of overall survival by a multi-omics-based clustering incorporating clinical and pathological features, genetic alterations, DNA methylation patterns, and the expression of mRNA, lncRNA, and microRNA, together with somatic mutations. These CSs differ significantly regarding their molecular alteration profiles and signaling pathways activation. Multi-omics-based clustering combined with machine learning algorithms, provides a risk score, considering 17 genes, for survival probability and likelihood of response to specific immunotherapies or chemotherapies, enabling individualized risk assessment and treatment recommendations.Two contributions address methodological gaps in AI-based prediction (Wang J.-W. et al., 2025, Xie S.-H. et al., 2025). A comprehensive review highlights a critical limitation in current machine learning applications for immunotherapy: the near-absence of causal inference (Wang J.-W. et al., 2025). Despite widespread use of deep learning, most models remain correlational and lack interpretability. The authors discuss emerging causal ML frameworks capable of distinguishing true causal effects from spurious associations, integrating multimodal data, and improving clinical applicability. They outline key challenges, data quality, algorithmic opacity, and interdisciplinary barriers, and propose pathways to bridge the knowledge-practice gap. A second study develops a machine learning model combining habitat imaging and Vision Transformer architectures to predict treatment response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in esophageal cancer (Xie S.-H. et al., 2025). Using data from six centers, the ExtraTrees model achieves high predictive performance and robust calibration. SHAP analyses enhance interpretability, offering a non-invasive tool to guide personalized treatment strategies.For ESCC, neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (nICT) represents a promising, innovative treatment strategy. A retrospective multicenter study (Xie S. et al., 2025) involving 306 ESCC patients undergoing nICT investigates the prognostic significance of major pathological response (MPR) compared to pathological complete response (pCR), which is currently classified as a surrogate endpoint for survival in studies of neoadjuvant therapy by the FDA. Regarding the primary endpoints recurrence-free survival and recurrence patterns, the results demonstrate that MPR has similar prognostic significance to pCR. Further, adjuvant therapy did not provide any additional recurrence-free benefits for MPR patients, suggesting that MPR could serve as a surrogate endpoint for pCR and potential influencing follow-up protocol. In 112 patients with locally advanced ESCC (LA-ESCC) who underwent nICT and adjuvant immunotherapy, it was demonstrated (Wu X. et al., 2025) that the combination of nICT and adjuvant immunotherapy offers short-term survival benefits and has an acceptable safety profile, which could represent an effective treatment strategy for LA-ESCC patients.Because patients with cancer face varying risk of recurrence tied to their clinical features and disease history, physicians are confronted with new challenges in tacking these prognostic issues. Researchers are suggesting innovative approaches that acknowledge the distinct characteristics of each patient and provide personalized therapies. Some researchers have considered nomograms for patients with gliomas (Zaho Y. et al. 2025), those with primary central nervous system germ cell tumors (Yao D. et al. 2025), and patients with HIV who have had curative resection for colorectal cancer (CC) (Li X. et al., 2026). Two studies have used the SEER database, as indicated in studies of Zaho Y. Other researchers have integrated lymphovascular and perineural invasion into the TNM staging of CC (iTNM, Hu J. et al., 2026) to improve prognostic accuracy and enable risk-adjusted therapeutic decision-making. Some authors adopted a different strategy by proposing novel biomarkers (like CHI3L1 for the study of Wang C. et al. 2025) or aggregating published studies in a metaanalysis emphasizing the significance of imaged parameters from PET/CT in predicting outcomes for patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma undergoing CAR-T cells therapy (Long C. et al., 2026). When analyzed in accordance with the methodological framework for the development and validation of predictive models, the six studies (Wang C. et al., 2025, Yao D. et al., 2025, Zaho Y. et al., 2025, Hu J et al.,, 2026, Li X. et al., 2026, Long C. et al., 2026) show a consistent progression. The nomograms in Li X. et al., 2026, Zaho Y. et al., 2025and Yao D, et al., 2025 followed the standard procedure: definition of the outcome measure (overall survival), predictors selection via multivariate regression, followed by an assessment of discriminatory power (an AUC of 0.935 for Li X. et al., 2026, C-index of 0.773/0.712 for Yao D. et al., 2025 and0.796/0.799 for Zaho Y. et al., 2025) followed by calibration curves (Yao D. et al., 2025), and decision curve analysis (Yao D. et al., 2025). In Hu J. et al., 2026, the N stage of the TNM classification (iTNM) is adjusted using a range of model comparison techniques including propensity score matching (PSM) to create balanced exposure, C-index, AUC, calibration, decision curve analysis (DCA), net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) to prove that reclassifying patients yields to meaningful benefit. Long C. et al., 2026 assessed PET/CT parameters (SUVmax, MTV, TMTV, TLG) in an alternative manner: considering them as prognostic factors rather than a model, using pooled hazard ratios with I² heterogeneity in a meta-analysis involving 14 studies. At last, Wang C. et al., 2025 validated the CHI3L1 biomarker using both clinical (diagnostic, Kaplan-Meier, Cox regression) and biological (serum ELISA dosage, RT-qPCR on PBMC, GEO and WGCNA datasets, and the protein-protein interaction network). For future predictive studies involving advanced or novel multimodal models, the roadmap has now been clearly outlined to ensure accurate cancer prognosis: define the clinical objective and the outcome measure, select the covariates, then evaluate each model according to its four core components -discrimination, calibration, internal validation (bootstrap for Li X. et al., 2026, andtraining/test cohorts for Zaho Y. et al., 2025), and clinical utility using DCA (only studies of Hu J. et al., 2026 andYao D. et al., 2025 combine calibration andDCA), ideally with an external validation (Yao D. et al. 2025).The thirteen contributions of this second volume collectively demonstrate how integrative approaches; spanning immunology, multi-omics, imaging, machine learning, and clinical validation; that hold promise for advancing prediction and decision-making in oncology. By addressing methodological gaps, refining biomarkers, and developing clinically actionable tools, these studies contribute to a more precise, interpretable, and personalized cancer care landscape. The editors thank all authors, reviewers, and contributors for their valuable work and for advancing the field through this Research Topic.

works.title: Neutralizing immunity across SARS-CoV-2 variants in kidney disease: broad deficits and sex-related heterogeneity after China’s Omicron wave
works.abstract: Background Variant-specific SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing responses in kidney disease (KD) remain incompletely characterized after China’s 2022–2023 Omicron wave. We compared these responses and their heterogeneity between participants with KD and healthy controls (HC) sampled in the same region. Methods This cross-sectional study included 380 participants: 197 HC and 183 participants with KD, sampled in Zhejiang Province from March to early April 2023. Pseudovirus assays measured neutralization against the prototype strain (PT), BA.4/5, and XBB.1.5. KD/HC geometric mean ratios (GMRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Group differences and interactions with sex, age, and vaccination-dose category were assessed using log 10 -transformed titers. Disease categories and confirmed infection before sampling were examined in exploratory analyses. Results KD participants had significantly lower titers against PT, BA.4/5, and XBB.1.5, with KD/HC GMRs of 0.167 (95% CI, 0.110–0.255), 0.491 (0.359–0.672), and 0.626 (0.489–0.802), respectively. Group-by-sex interactions were significant for all three viruses (interaction P = 0.0006, 0.0163, and 0.0067, respectively), with larger relative HC–KD differences among women. Receipt of ≥3 doses, compared with 0–2 doses, was associated with higher PT titers in both groups, whereas no significant overall dose associations were detected for BA.4/5 or XBB.1.5. No significant group interactions with age or vaccination-dose category were detected. Exploratory analyses showed lower PT and BA.4/5 titers in glomerular/immune-mediated than in metabolic/vascular kidney disease. In the questionnaire subgroup, confirmed infection before sampling was associated with higher BA.4/5 titers without a significant group-by-infection interaction. Conclusions KD was associated with lower neutralization across all three viruses, with consistently larger relative HC–KD differences among women. These findings highlight sex-related heterogeneity in post-wave neutralizing immunity and support prospective studies integrating renal phenotype, treatment, vaccination history, and clinical outcomes.

works.title: Bidirectional interactions between HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibodies and natural killer cells in antibody development and effector phases: a systematic review
works.abstract: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) are increasingly investigated for HIV-1 prevention and treatment. bNAbs have both direct neutralizing activity and Fc-dependent effector functions. Natural killer (NK) cells are important Fc-dependent effectors, but their interactions with bNAbs remain incompletely understood. This systematic review evaluated the bidirectional relationship between NK cells and HIV-1 bNAbs, focusing on natural bNAb development and interactions involving mature bNAbs. Following PRISMA 2020, PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from inception through August 10, 2026. A total of 40 studies met the eligibility criteria. Findings were synthesized narratively because of substantial heterogeneity. Evidence on the role of NK cells in bNAb development was limited and mainly observational. NK cell subset distribution, RAB11FIP5 expression, degranulation, and cytokine responses were associated with neutralization breadth, without establishing causality. Evidence was stronger for the effector phase. bNAbs induced NK cell degranulation and cytokine production and mediated NK cell-dependent killing of infected cells. These responses varied among bNAbs and were influenced by antibody properties, NK cell subset and differentiation phenotype, and viral, target cell, microenvironmental, and experimental factors. Enhanced NK cell activity did not necessarily translate into greater protection in vivo . The evidence provides stronger support for NK cell effector responses involving mature bNAbs, whereas a causal role for NK cells in natural bNAb development remains unestablished. Future studies should clarify whether NK cells causally influence bNAb development and under what conditions NK cell engagement provides additional antiviral benefit beyond direct neutralization. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/ , identifier CRD420261378840.

works.title: ISM1 promotes alveolar fluid clearance in acute lung injury by targeting cell-surface GRP78 and inhibiting PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway
works.abstract: Introduction Impaired alveolar fluid clearance (AFC) is a major pathological feature of acute lung injury (ALI). The epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and Na + /K + -ATPase are the principal ion transport proteins that mediate AFC. Isthmin-1 (ISM1), a secreted protein with diverse biological functions, has been reported to protect against ALI; however, whether this protective effect is mediated through modulation of AFC remains unknown. This study aimed to elucidate the role and mechanism of ISM1 in regulating AFC in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced ALI. Methods In vivo , ISM1 was overexpressed in mice using an adeno-associated virus serotype 5 (AAV5) vector, and an anti-GRP78 blocking antibody was administered to neutralize cell-surface GRP78 function. In vitro , LPS-stimulated A549 cells were treated with recombinant ISM1 protein, anti-GRP78 antibody, or the PI3K activator 740Y-P. The severity of ALI was assessed by hematoxylin-eosin staining, lung wet/dry weight ratio, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid total protein concentration, and inflammatory cytokine levels. α-ENaC and Na + /K + -ATPase α1 expression were evaluated by Western blot, RT-qPCR, and immunofluorescence, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway activity was analyzed in both models. Results ISM1 overexpression attenuated LPS-induced ALI, as shown by reduced lung injury scores, lung wet/dry weight ratios, BALF total protein concentrations, and inflammatory cytokine levels, together with upregulated α-ENaC and Na + /K + -ATPase α1 expression. Mechanistically, ISM1 promoted α-ENaC and Na + /K + -ATPase α1 expression by suppressing the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway, and these effects were significantly attenuated by GRP78 blockade. Conclusions These findings suggest that ISM1 promotes alveolar fluid clearance and protects against ALI through a GRP78-dependent mechanism involving inhibition of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, suggesting that ISM1 may have protective effects against ALI.

works.title: Editorial: Bacterial strategies to evade immune responses: oxidative and nutritional stress as key factors in host-pathogen crosstalk
works.abstract: Two Original Research articles broaden the interaction between two bacterial species, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Mycoplasma genitalium with neutrophils. Fretes et al., investigated P. gingivalis, a periodontal pathogen associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes that actively release outer membrane vesicles (PgOMV) and provides particularly relevant evidence of how bacterial-derived factors can modify immune-cell antimicrobial functions and metabolism. The authors investigate whether these vesicles modify human neutrophil activation, extracellular antimicrobial mechanisms, metabolicassociated parameters, and bacterial internalization and persistence. They found that PgOMV activated neutrophils, raising ROS production and CD11b expression, However, this response was not accompanied by the induction of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Instead, PgOMVs reduced extracellular DNA through DNase activity, including the degradation of DNA in previously generated NET preparations. This observation suggests that bacterial vesicles can interfere with an important extracellular antimicrobial mechanism even in the presence of cellular activation signals.PgOMV shifted neutrophil metabolism: glucose uptake and lipid droplets increased, lactate release dropped, and mitochondrial mass and membrane potential declined.Neutrophils pre-exposed to PgOMV internalized more P. gingivalis and allowed it to persist longer, and the medium they conditioned reduced migration of trophoblastic cells. Vesicles from bacteria grown under H2O2 stress activated neutrophils to a similar degree but left glucose uptake and lactate release unchanged, and they promoted even greater bacterial internalization and persistence than basal vesicles. Thus, exposure to bacterial vesicles appears to promote an activated but permissive cellular phenotype, in which some activation-associated responses coexist with impaired extracellular antimicrobial activity and enhanced bacterial persistence. These findings suggest that the oxidative environment encountered by bacteria can modify the biological properties of their vesicles and, consequently, the way in which host immune cells respond to them.Another Original Article, by Tian et al., explored M. genitalium, a recognized cause of sexually transmitted infections that can persist in the female reproductive tract. In these tissues it is associated with cervicitis marked by neutrophil infiltration. The authors show that infected endocervical epithelial cells upregulate IL-33 that once in the nucleus, could associate with the NF-κB subunit p65 and help it drive production of the chemokines CXCL1 and IL-8. These chemokines, in turn, were needed for neutrophils to adhere, migrate, and become activated. The authors suggested a mechanism in which M. genitalium co-opts the intranuclear role of IL-33 to sustain neutrophil-driven inflammation, which may help explain the tissue damage seen in chronic infection.These findings nevertheless provide a valuable basis for investigating how pathogens interact with epithelial regulatory mechanisms to shape innate immune responses at reproductive mucosal interfaces.Taken together, these two articles showed how these two bacterial species impact neutrophile physiology may influence not only their own survival but also their capacity to reprogram host immunity.One of the most important strategies to boost the immune system is vaccination, however for many bacterial species there is no available vaccine. Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis (S. Enteritidis) is a leading global cause of foodborne infection, and the emergence of multidrug-resistant strains has complicated the clinical scenario.Central carbon metabolism is key for bacterial survival, Zhu et al., investigated the role of gltA, which encodes citrate synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme initiating the TCA cycle. A deletion mutant, ΔgltA, showed lower motility and biofilm formation by inhibiting curli fimbriae and cellulose synthesis, and increased susceptibility to antimicrobial agents. The ΔgltA mutant also showed reduced tolerance to gastric stresses. Particularly relevant to the scope of this Research Topic, the mutant showed diminished resistance to oxidative stress, in addition to acidic, alkaline, thermal, and osmotic challenges. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed extensive changes in gene expression, including the downregulation of several virulence-associated genes.The intraperitoneal infection with the mutant strain showed decreased organ bacterial loads and global downregulation of virulence genes. A single oral immunization with ΔgltA elicited robust humoral and cellular immunity, in mice, serving as a promising candidate strain and molecular target for further development of live attenuated S.Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium considered a global health threat.Two Original Research contributions addressed different aspects of S. aureus physiology. Feng et al., conducted a retrospective study of 321 S. aureus bloodstream infection patients to analyze in-hospital mortality and its predictors. Mortality was considerable and higher in infections caused by methicillin-resistant strains than by susceptible ones, and a large share of deaths clustered within the first days, leaving a very narrow window for intervention. On the host side, older age, systemic severity at presentation, a pulmonary source and a pronounced inflammatory response, reflected in elevated neutrophil levels and procalcitonin, were each independently linked to death. On the pathogen side, methicillin resistance and ineffective or absent antibiotic therapy worsened prognosis.The second work, by An et al., investigated the role of small colony variants (SCVs) of S. aureus in pulmonary infection in China where the information is still scarce. The authors compared SCVs with normal-phenotype strains recovered from the lower airways of patients with Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia, characterizing their resistance profiles, molecular typing, virulence genes, biofilm formation, serum resistance and behavior in a mice model of lung infection. SCVs were uncommon among isolates, but a large proportion were methicillin-resistant, and they more often carried genes associated with immune evasion and formed strong biofilms. They also withstood host serum better and, in mice, sustained higher bacterial burden, inflammation and lung damage at late stages. Patients with SCVs received more fluoroquinolones and mechanical ventilation and stayed longer in hospital.It is interesting to consider that the SCVs are selected under oxidative pressure, for example during chronic infections due to immune system response and in presence of P. aeruginosa toxins (Biswas et al., 2009). These variants arise mainly from mutation in the respiratory chain components, like menadione and hemin, and S. aureus undergoes to a fermentative metabolism that makes the bacteria very difficult to eradicate (Biswas et al., 2009).The former works investigated different aspects of bacterial pathogens survival strategies evading immune responses and/or adapting to the hostile conditions they meet once infection is established. The mini review by Gasior et al., explored the stringent response that is key for bacterial survival and adaptation. In this process, the alarmones (p)ppGpp, reprogram bacterial gene expression and metabolism so that cells can endure stresses typical of the host environment, including nutrient limitation and oxidative attack. Because this pathway lets pathogens withstand host-imposed pressure, and because antibiotic resistance keeps eroding conventional options, it is an appealing target for new antimicrobial approaches.An important perspective emerging from this Research Topic is the need to integrate bacterial metabolic adaptation with the functional state of host immune cells. The ability of bacteria to resist oxidative stress, modify their metabolic pathways, or release vesicles with immunomodulatory properties may influence the effectiveness of immunemediated elimination. This reciprocal interaction is particularly relevant in tissues exposed to persistent or recurrent microbial challenges, where prolonged inflammation and incomplete pathogen clearance may contribute to tissue dysfunction.

works.title: Activated TILs are restricted by iron availability in pancreatic cancer
Engineered stem cell-derived CD16-enhanced universal NKT cells improve monoclonal antibody-based cancer immunotherapy
works.abstract: Monoclonal antibody (mAb)-based therapies have revolutionized cancer treatment; however, their clinical efficacy is often limited by insufficient antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), tumor antigen escape, and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). To overcome these limitations, we developed an allogeneic stem cell-derived invariant natural killer T (NKT) cell platform engineered to express a high-affinity non-cleavable CD16 receptor (CD16HSC-NKT) for broad enhancement of mAb-based immunotherapy. Using a clinically guided differentiation platform, we generated highly pure and scalable CD16HSC-NKT cells exhibiting robust expression of NK receptors, potent cytotoxic machinery, and a Th1-biased cytokine profile. CD16HSC-NKT cells demonstrated potent intrinsic antitumor activity and potently enhanced the efficacy of multiple therapeutic antibodies, including Trastuzumab, Tafasitamab, Rituximab, Daratumumab, and Cusatuzumab, across diverse hematologic and solid tumor models. In vivo, combination therapy induced durable tumor eradication and prolonged survival in xenograft models, outperforming the clinically approved antibody-drug conjugate trastuzumab deruxtecan. Mechanistically, therapeutic antibodies promoted the expansion, persistence, and activation of CD16HSC-NKT cells within tumors. CD16HSC-NKT uniquely remodeled the TME by selectively depleting CD1d-expressing tumor-associated macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells. CD16HSC-NKT cells also exhibited minimal alloreactivity, no graft-versus-host disease, and no detectable systemic toxicity. Collectively, these findings establish CD16HSC-NKT cells as a safe, off-the-shelf cellular platform capable of broadly enhancing monoclonal antibody therapy through sustained ADCC, multimodal tumor targeting, and TME remodeling.

works.title: A Library of Potent TCRs Derived from Healthy Donors Targeting Kras G12d and G12v Neoantigens
works.abstract: Kirsten rat sarcoma (KRAS), the most frequently altered oncogene, is a key target for T cell-based therapies. Mutant KRAS (mKRAS)-specific T cell receptors (TCRs) enable targeted treatment for patients with matching mKRAS/HLA allele pairs. We generated a TCR warehouse library covering approximately one-quarter of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients and 10% of colorectal cancer patients. Warehouse TCRs exhibit strong avidities and cytotoxicity, comparable to existing benchmark TCRs. Detailed characterization of each TCR revealed unique biology for specific KRAS neoantigens. TCRs with high sensitivity for KRAS G12V/HLA-C*01:02 also recognize the wild-type epitope. However, the wild-type epitope abundance appears to be significantly lower, potentially creating a therapeutic window, albeit necessitating deeper evaluation. Additionally, we show that TCRs recognize KRAS G12V on HLA-C*03:03 and HLA-C*03:04 interchangeably, thereby resulting in a single neoantigen with one of the highest frequencies. In summary, this mKRAS-targeted TCR library comprises candidates for further preclinical and clinical development.

The structural basis of IL-36R proinflammatory signaling mediated by IL-36γ and IL-37
works.abstract: The interleukin-36 receptor (IL-36R) drives proinflammatory signaling and is therapeutically targeted by spesolimab in acute skin inflammation. Beyond its three canonical agonists (IL-36α, IL-36β, and IL-36γ), IL-36R was recently proposed to be activated by IL-37. Together with antagonism by IL-36R antagonist (IL-36RA) and IL-38, this creates a complex structure-function landscape that remains poorly understood. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of human IL-36γ bound to IL-36R and the shared co-receptor IL-1R accessory protein (IL-1RAcP). IL-36γ engages IL-36R with low affinity, enabling high-affinity IL-1RAcP recruitment. IL-37 exhibits the opposite binding signature, binding IL-36R with high affinity but IL-1RAcP weakly. Functional comparison of IL-36R engagement by IL-36γ and IL-37 confirmed their common proinflammatory signature, with IL-36γ exhibiting markedly higher potency, consistent with its more stable signaling complex. Structural comparison of cytokine-bound versus antibody-antagonized IL-36R revealed that spesolimab acts as an allosteric antagonist. This study therefore provides a structural and mechanistic blueprint for IL-36R activation by distinct cytokines.

works.title: Programming immunity in situ: A new frontier of in vivo cell engineering
works.abstract: In vivo cell engineering enables the direct programming of immune cells inside patients. Instead of isolating, modifying, and reinfusing cells, therapeutic instructions are delivered directly to selected immune cells through lipid nanoparticles or viral vectors. This approach could facilitate rapid and scalable deployment of varied immune cell therapies across disease contexts. Early clinical studies in oncology and autoimmunity demonstrate increasing technical and clinical feasibility. The next challenge lies in enhancing precision to ensure that vectors reach the target cell type and tissue, deliver the appropriate payload, and produce desired transient or durable activity. Progress in targeting ligands, vector design, biodistribution control, and genome editing is beginning to address these barriers. Ensuring safety against immunogenicity, inflammatory toxicity, off-target editing, and uncontrolled persistence remains a central priority. By mastering these constraints, in vivo engineering could turn endogenous immune cells into therapeutic agents generated directly in the body, expanding cell therapy to diseases refractory to current modalities.

works.title: T-cell immunity in anti-tumor battle
works.abstract: Abstract The clinical success of T-cell-based immunotherapies has transformed oncology, yet tumor immune evasion remains a formidable barrier. In this review, we delineate the developmental and molecular landscapes that shape antitumor T-cell immunity. Following a brief overview of CD4 + helper T-cell contributions, we focus primarily on CD8 + cytotoxic lineages. Rather than a passive loss of effector function, CD8 + T-cell exhaustion is increasingly recognized as functional attrition and profound oligoclonality. In the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), unremitting antigenic pressure drives an iterative selection process that` narrows a highly diverse T-cell pool into a constricted, oligoclonal population, a phenomenon termed “clonal contraction”. We expand the conceptual scale of T-cell clonal selection during the immune response, tracing this clonal evolution from early thymic selection and primary antigen priming to exhaustive terminal differentiation. We further propose a structural model demonstrating how the biophysical constraints of a fixed T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire create a profound imbalance against rapidly diversifying tumor antigens. Within this framework, we highlight tissue-resident memory (Trm) as a crucial spatial reservoir that safeguards the host against the depletion of functional clones. Finally, we contextualize the therapeutic paradigm of immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) and note that, under some circumstances, durable clinical efficacy can be driven by systemic “clonal replacement”. Ultimately, we argue that next-generation T-cell-based immunotherapies may shift `from attempting only to reverse functional exhaustion to actively engineering continuous clonal selection and preserving TCR repertoire diversity.

works.title: Deubiquitinases at the crossroads of T-cell immunity and tumor immune evasion
works.abstract: The T-cell-mediated antitumor immune response has emerged as a key axis for controlling cancer growth and progression, as shown by the widespread success of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Unfortunately, ICB therapy still fails in a large percentage of patients, and there is a growing need to identify novel targets to increase anticancer immunity and enhance existing treatments. Among emerging therapeutic targets, deubiquitinases (DUBs) have attracted increasing attention because of their central role in regulating ubiquitin signaling. As key components of the ubiquitin system, DUBs catalyze the removal of ubiquitin from substrate proteins, thereby dynamically reversing ubiquitination and fine-tuning protein stability, localization, activity, and protein‒protein interactions. Accumulating evidence indicates that DUBs regulate not only tumor-intrinsic pathways that promote immune evasion but also T-cell activation, differentiation, and effector function, positioning them as promising therapeutic targets at the interface between cancer and immunity. However, DUBs are rarely considered holistically involved in both T-cell immunity and tumor-intrinsic immune evasion, despite the growing appreciation that individual DUBs often act in both compartments. In this review, we comprehensively examine the roles of DUBs in T-cell immunity and tumor-intrinsic immune evasion and discuss perspectives on therapeutic strategies targeting DUBs along this axis.

Bcl11a preserves hematopoietic stem cell function in culture by restraining Ncf1-dependent ROS
works.abstract: Ex vivo expansion of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) is limited by culture-induced oxidative stress, yet the upstream transcriptional drivers remain poorly defined. Here, we show that the transcription factor Bcl11a is rapidly and persistently downregulated during HSC culture and that this decline drives functional deterioration. Bcl11a was both required and sufficient to maintain quiescence, clonogenic activity, and serially transplantable HSC function. Mechanistically, Bcl11a directly represses a Nox2 NADPH oxidase gene module, including Ncf1, encoding the p47phox organizer subunit; Ncf1 deletion reduced ROS and partially rescued the defects of Bcl11a-deficient HSCs. Rapamycin-but not the ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine-restored Bcl11a expression, suppressed Ncf1 and ROS, and improved HSC function, identifying Bcl11a as a candidate effector linking mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 inhibition to redox control. This axis was conserved in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, revealing a druggable transcriptional vulnerability of cultured HSCs and a framework for improving ex vivo-expanded grafts.

works.abstract: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) in tumors are associated with improved responses to immunotherapy. Here, we examined the impact of type 1 conventional dendritic cells (cDC1s) in TLS formation. Reprogrammed tumor cells into cDC1-like cells remodeled the tumor microenvironment and induced immunogenic TLSs (imgTLSs) across melanoma, colon, bladder, breast, and pancreatic cancer models with distinct genetic backgrounds. cDC1-like cells activated lymphotoxin, TNF, and interferon programs and engaged early with T cells through MHC class I and CD40 signaling to induce imgTLSs containing BCL6 + germinal centers, independently of endogenous cDC1s. Intratumoral positioning shaped distinct cDC1-like cell states, with DC-LAMP + CCR7 + migratory cDC1s nucleating niches enriched in CD4 + , CD8 + T cells, and B cells in mouse and human tumors. ImgTLSs sustained B and T cell responses and promoted systemic immunity through expansion of shared clonotypes in distant, untreated tumors. Our findings outline the spatial organization, signaling programs and interactions of cDC1-like cells that initiate intratumoral lymphoid structures and establish cellular reprogramming as a strategy toward overcoming resistance to immunotherapy.

works.abstract: Trained immunity describes the capacity of innate immune cells to develop memory-like responses following a prior challenge. Early studies focused on myeloid cells and bone marrow progenitors. Extension of this concept to mucosal tissues, however, presents a more complex picture. These barrier sites harbor diverse, long-lived immune populations that interact with structural cells and neuronal circuits to actively shape immune responses. Emerging evidence suggests that memory-like programs extend beyond immune cells to include epithelial, stromal, and neuronal compartments. We propose that trained immunity in mucosal surfaces is distributed across the tissue ecosystem, encompassing progenitors, tissue-resident populations, and the tissue niche. This expanded framework redefines innate immune memory and has important implications for infections and chronic inflammatory diseases.

Posttranslational Modifications of Unconventional Autoantigens: Shaping Immunogenicity and Inflammatory Activity
works.abstract: Posttranslational modifications (PTMs) of self-antigens precipitate autoimmunity by generating neo-epitopes that breach tolerance and activate autoreactive T and B cells. This review spotlights cathelicidin LL37 and chemokine CXCL4 (PF4) in psoriatic disease (psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, PSO and PSA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and systemic sclerosis (SSc), drawing on key studies including our own. Uniquely, unlike most autoantigens, LL37 and CXCL4 exert a dual role: they are immunogenic targets for T and B cells while directly fueling innate inflammation. Through chaperone-like binding to self- and microbial DNA/RNA, they form complexes that potently stimulate plasmacytoid and myeloid dendritic cells (pDCs/mDCs) via DNA/RNA sensors, such as TLR7-9 and cGAS/STING, driving Type I interferon and cytokines storms. Strikingly, these complexes also induce B cells to become antibody-producing plasma cells, amplifying adaptive responses and likely suppressing regulation. Here, we detail the role of PTM-modified LL37 in PSO, PSA, and SLE-forming autoantigenic neutrophil extracellular traps-and CXCL4 in SSc, where it acts as biomarker and autoantibody target. Our work underscores how this dual functionality as "bifunctional autoantigens" exacerbates disease, and how PTMs modification influence these phenomena. These molecules and their PTM can be targeted to halt inflammatory cascades and restore tolerance.

works.title: Diet-independent pregravid obesity drives premature but functionally dysregulated fetal immune maturation across multiple immune compartments in rhesus macaques
works.abstract: Pregravid obesity is associated with long-term immune alterations in offspring, but the mechanisms linking maternal metabolic state to fetal immune development remain poorly defined. To address this gap, we used a rhesus macaque model of spontaneous, diet-independent pregravid obesity to examine impact of pregravid obesity on fetal immune maturation and function. We profiled immune cell frequency, function, transcriptional programs, and inferred intercellular communication in umbilical cord blood, fetal spleen, and fetal lung using spectral flow cytometry, multiplex cytokine profiling, functional stimulation assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing. Pregravid obesity was associated with altered fetal organ growth, elevated inflammatory mediators, altered immune cell frequencies, and hyperresponsive splenic leukocyte responses to in vitro stimulation. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed a conserved program of innate immune reprogramming across all three compartments, characterized by heightened inflammatory, migratory, and metabolic signatures together with reduced antigen-presentation potential. We also observed impaired T cell maturation with premature effector differentiation and evidence of B cell dysfunction. Computationally inferred cell-cell communication predicted loss of tolerogenic signaling and enhanced proinflammatory pathways across splenic and lung myeloid cells. Together, these findings indicate that diet-independent pregravid obesity drives premature but functionally dysregulated maturation of fetal circulating and tissue-resident immune cells, providing a candidate mechanism for the increased susceptibility to infection, respiratory disease, and immune dysregulation reported in offspring of mothers with obesity. This connection should be tested directly in postnatal studies.

works.title: IL-9 signaling requires ornithine decarboxylase-dependent polyamine metabolism in macrophages to promote allergic airway inflammation
works.abstract: macrophages contribute to allergic airway inflammation is still lacking. Here, we found that IL-9R-deficiency reduced arginine-dependent polyamine metabolism. Polyamines were required effectors as myeloid cell deficiency of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC1), the gateway enzyme to polyamine synthesis, decreased the expansion of interstitial macrophages and attenuated allergic airway inflammation. Pulmonary supplementation of polyamines rescued allergic inflammation in IL-9R-deficient mice. Expression of CCL24 that augments eosinophil recruitment into the lung environment required both IL-9R signaling and ODC1 activity in lung macrophages. Moreover, targeting of macrophage CCL24 using nanoparticles loaded with a Ccl24 siRNA inhibited allergic airway inflammation. Thus, our study reveals an IL-9R/macrophage/polyamine/CCL24 axis in lung macrophage populations and identifies polyamine biosynthesis as a potential therapeutic target for allergic airway inflammation.

works.title: From disease prevention to transmission blocking: Building the translational pathway for mucosal respiratory vaccines
The altered T cell landscape in systemic sclerosis patients is characterized by dysfunctional type 1 immunity
works.abstract: T cells in patients with chronic autoimmunity show features of dysfunction. However, the functionally defined T cell subsets that are affected by these changes remain poorly characterized. Here, we sought to reveal aberrations in the composition, phenotype, and function of canonical T cell subsets in the blood of systemic sclerosis (SSc) patients compared with healthy subjects and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients. Therefore, we developed a novel multidimensional flow-cytometry panel to simultaneously detect lineage-defining transcription factors, co-inhibitory receptors and other functional markers to characterize T cell subsets without in vitro restimulation. We compared T cell landscapes in SSc and SLE patients, and healthy subjects, using opt-SNE (optimized t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) and PhenoGraph algorithms. The data show altered distribution and aberrant functional states of transcription factor-defined T cell subsets in patients with autoimmunity, with shared and unique features between diseases and their subtypes. Strikingly, SSc and SLE patients showed deficiencies in subsets of CD8+ and CD4-CD8- T cells that expressed T-bet, which is critical for IFN-γ-dependent type 1 immunity. Moreover, TIGIT+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells, which suppress T helper 1 responses, were increased in diffuse cutaneous SSc and SLE patients. Functionally, T cells from SSc patients produced less IFN-γ, a cytokine that suppresses profibrotic gene expression in fibroblasts, as we demonstrate by transcriptomic analysis. Our study supports a model in which IFN-γ opposes canonical fibrotic gene programs in fibroblasts, and deficiencies in the IFN-γ-producing T cell compartment in SSc patients therefore may contribute to chronic fibrosis development. Aberrant T cell subsets in SSc and SLE represent targets for corrective immunotherapy.

works.title: TLR2 expression by B and myeloid cells contributes to the antibody response against Francisella tularensis lipoproteins
works.abstract: Bacterial lipoproteins are potent TLR2 agonists with significant immunogenic activity. However, it is unclear how TLR2 expression by B cells or other cell types can contribute to the humoral response against these Ags. Here, we demonstrate that the immunogenicity of Francisella tularensis lipoproteins Tul4 and FTT1103, in the absence of adjuvant, depends on their lipid moieties and, in part, on TLR2. Intraperitoneal immunization with Tul4 and FTT1103 elicits both T-dependent and T-independent Ab production, with TLR2 expression by B cells being critical for the T-independent production of IgM and IgG3. TLR2 expression by B cells and myeloid cells, but not T cells, played a major role in promoting T-dependent IgM and IgG production, except IgG1, whose induction was TLR2 independent. Mice immunized with Tul4 or FTT1103 were protected against tularemia, whereas immunization with the deacylated proteins was ineffective. Our study demonstrates, for the first time, to our knowledge, that B cell-intrinsic TLR2 expression is important for the humoral response against bacterial lipoproteins. These results may help in the design of more sophisticated vaccines against tularemia and other infections.

works.title: Interleukin-15 complex–induced interleukin-10 acts on brain endothelial cells to reduce CD8 T-cell arrest during cerebral malaria
works.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a life-threatening complication of Plasmodium infection driven in part by an overwhelming inflammatory response. No clinical therapies are approved that specifically prevent immunopathology during CM. In experimental cerebral malaria (ECM), vascular endothelial cells in the mouse brain cross-present malaria antigen and upregulate adhesion molecules in response to inflammation. This causes CD8 T-cell arrest, activation, and lethal disruption of the blood-brain barrier. We previously reported that treatment with IL-15 cytokine complex (IL-15C) prevents ECM by inducing natural killer (NK) cell secretion of IL-10. To further uncover the mechanisms underlying this immunotherapy, OT-I T cells were transferred into mice, followed by infection with ovalbumin-expressing Plasmodium berghei. Using intravital microscopy, we observed major areas of OT-I arrest within the brains of untreated mice experiencing ECM. IL-15C treatment reduced the number of arresting OT-I T cells, coinciding with an increased mean velocity when compared to untreated mice. To identify the target of NK cell-secreted IL-10, we used conditional knockouts of IL-10Rα and found that protection from ECM occurs through IL-10Rα on endothelial cells and not CD8 T cells. Coinciding with this, IL-15C reduced the expression of adhesion molecules, selectins, and MHC-I on brain endothelial cells. In summary, our studies support the mechanism that IL-15C treatment reduces the number of arrested CD8 T cells along the cerebral vasculature by modulating endothelial cells to prevent ECM. These insights demonstrate the potential for treatments that reduce T-cell arrest to improve outcomes of human CM.

works.title: The role of NLRC5 in human inflammatory bowel diseases and murine experimental colitis
works.abstract: Nucleotide-binding, leucine-rich repeat-containing (NLR) innate immune proteins have been implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). NLRC5 is a key trans-activator of class I MHC (MHC-I) genes, but it is also found to regulate cytokines and cell death. Meta-analysis of 14 different human RNAseq or microarray data (total n = 1,093) revealed a consistent and strong association between IBD and heightened NLRC5 expression, suggesting a role for NLRC5 across diverse IBD patients. Furthermore, these data show a strong correlation of NLRC5 with inflammation and STAT1 signatures, suggesting that its role in human IBD may extend beyond its canonical role as a regulator of MHC-I, or that its expression is controlled by inflammation/STAT1. However, in the dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mouse model, Nlrc5 protected against colitis, which mimicked B2m-/- mice lacking MHC-I. This Nlrc5-associated protection has been consistent across hundreds of mice over a decade in the hands of several investigators. Microbiome study found significant alterations in the microbiota in overall composition and strain-specific differences over time, suggesting a dynamic relationship between microbiome dysbiosis and Nlrc5. To resolve these issues, we studied germ-free (GF) wild-type and Nlrc5-/- mice. Surprisingly, GF mice showed that Nlrc5 exacerbated instead of protected against DSS-induced colitis. A major difference between GF and conventionally-raised mice is that DSS reduced Nlrc5/ 2m expression in GF mice, while it did the opposite in SPF mice. These data highlight the complex role of Nlrc5 and the microbiome in the pathogenesis of IBD, as well as the necessity of complementary mouse models.

works.title: TNFR2 agonism increases tissue and effector Treg cells
works.abstract: Autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are driven by chronic inflammation and tissue damage. Regulatory T (Treg) cells are critical for maintaining immune tolerance, yet their therapeutic use is limited by stability and tissue homing. Here, we demonstrate that agonism of tumor necrosis factor receptor 2 (TNFR2) increases effector and tissue-competent Treg cell progenitors in mice and humans. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that TNFR2 is highly expressed on early and late nonlymphoid tissue Treg cell precursors, with expression strongly correlated with the BATF-driven tissue Treg cell transcriptional program. In vivo, a single dose of TNFR2 agonist promotes the clonal commitment of Treg cells to effector and tissue lineage, increasing tissue Treg cell populations in lymphoid and peripheral tissues. This increase is associated with enhanced suppressive function, epigenetic stability (preserved FOXP3 CNS2 demethylation), and resistance to inflammatory conversion. In murine models of skin inflammation and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, TNFR2 agonism ameliorates disease severity in a dose-dependent manner. Critically, in human Treg cells, TNFR2 agonism induces elements of the tissue residency transcriptional program-including upregulation of LAYN, CCR8, CCR4, and TIGIT-while maintaining lineage stability. These findings establish TNFR2 signaling as a central driver of effector and tissue Treg cell differentiation and position TNFR2 agonism as a transformative strategy for generating stable, tissue-competent effector Treg cells as a promising immunomodulatory therapy for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.

works.title: The development and validation of an IL-1β fate-mapping mouse unveils unexpected heterogeneity in innate immunity
works.abstract: Abstract Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) is a highly proinflammatory cytokine whose synthesis and cleavage are tightly regulated. It is important for protection from several infections, but can also play a damaging role in autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases. While pattern recognition receptor activation leads to potent induction of IL-1β, its production at steady state and the nature of cells that make IL-1β in vivo is not fully understood. Therefore, tools to detect early transcription of IL-1β–producing cells and permanent labeling of the lineage can provide critical insights into the functioning of the innate immune system. Here, we describe a novel IGNITE (IL-1β-Guided Neon green with Irreversible tdTomato Expression) mouse, a dual-reporter model that enables real-time visualization of Il1b transcription via mNeonGreen and permanent lineage tracing through Cre-dependent tdTomato expression. Using this system, we tracked Il1b-associated mNeonGreen and subsequent tdTomato expression both in vitro and in vivo. Unexpectedly, we identified heterogeneous tdTomato cell populations across multiple tissues in unmanipulated IGNITE mice, suggesting that a subset of myeloid cells transcribes Il1b at homeostasis without needing an experimentally driven activation of pattern recognition receptors. Neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells had different tdTomato+ proportions, suggesting varied encounters with inflammatory stimuli. Transcriptomic analysis revealed an unexpected dichotomy in the induction of NF-κB– versus IRF-mediated genes between tdTomato+ and tdTomato− conventional dendritic cell type 2 populations, following Toll-like receptor stimulation. Thus, the IGNITE mouse provides a powerful new tool for studying Il1b transcriptional dynamics and fate mapping, offering new insights into the spatial and temporal regulation of innate immune responses.

works.title: The metabolic reprogramming of T cells controls airway remodeling in severe asthma
works.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
works.abstract: Background: Mixed granulocytic asthma (MGA) is a severe Th2-low endotype, characterized by high Th17/neutrophilic burden and exacerbated airway remodeling.Both features confer resistance to inhaled corticosteroids and typical asthma treatments.Objective: We aimed to address gaps in knowledge, including how Th17 cells induce pathological tissue remodeling and how Th17 differentiation occurs in response to allergens. Methods:We generated a Th2-low murine model of asthma on the Il4rα -/-background that mimics the decrease in type 2 response seen in corticosteroid-resistant patients.We monitored major features of human disease including heightened airway reactivity to methacholine, Th17/neutrophilic inflammation, airway remodeling, and resistance to corticosteroid treatment.Comparative transfer of Th2 versus Th17 cells were analyzed.We further investigated how the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) pathway modulates pathogenic Th17 cell reprogramming by in vitro T cell cultures and in vivo therapeutic blockades.Results: LIGHT (aka TNFSF14) and the OXPHOS pathway are enriched in human MGA and likewise upregulated in this mouse model.We show OXPHOS promotes the metabolic reprograming of Th17 cells, to sustain their survival despite steroid treatment and produce LIGHT that controls airway remodeling.Mechanistically, OXPHOS regulates RORγt expression and the subsequent transcriptional network to program differentiation of Th17 cells, whereas LIGHT drives airway remodeling by activating the MMP9-dependent TGFβ pathway.Additionally, OXPHOS + Th17 cells promote the expression of osteopontin necessary for fibroblast activation.LIGHT antagonistic blockade reduces airway remodeling, whereas OXPHOS inhibition kills Th17 cells and subsequent neutrophilia.Importantly, the dual blockade of LIGHT and OXPHOS reverses all features of MGA back to baseline and reciprocally increases the numbers of Treg cells.Conclusions: The dual blockade of LIGHT and OXPHOS constitutes a promising target for clinical interventions in human MGA, possibly extending to other Th17-driven fibrotic diseases. J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o fKey Messages:• OXPHOS regulates RORγt expression and programming of pathogenic Th17 cells that are resistant to apoptosis.• Th17-derived LIGHT promotes airway remodeling by regulating MMP9-activation of TGF, and its inhibition reverses disease.• LIGHT and OXPHOS concomitant blockade, post-disease onset, abolishes central features of severe asthma including Th17/neutrophilic burden, airway remodeling, and airway hyperreactivity to methacholine. Capsule summary:OXPHOS-programmed Th17 cells produce LIGHT to control pathological remodeling.The combinatorial blockade of LIGHT/OXPHOS offers a novel therapeutic strategy to treat Th17driven fibrotic diseases, including severe asthma. works.title: Persistent indirect airway hyperresponsiveness after six weeks of high-dose inhaled corticosteroids identifies a subgroup with higher T2 inflammation and mast cell burden
works.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
works.abstract: Background Indirect airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) to osmotic stimuli such as mannitol is a hallmark of asthma and typically improves with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), in contrast to direct AHR stimuli (e.g. methacholine), which often persists despite treatment. Persistent indirect AHR (PIAHR) after high-dose ICS may reflect incomplete suppression of airway inflammation. Objective We aimed to characterise clinical, inflammatory, and tissue features associated with persistent indirect AHR in patients with asthma before and after high-dose ICS treatment. Methods This post-hoc analysis of the RECONSTRUCT study included corticosteroid-free patients with asthma and AHR to mannitol. Participants underwent examinations, including bronchoscopy, before and after six weeks of treatment with 1600 μg inhaled budesonide daily. Patients were stratified as responders (abolished AHR; PD 15 ≥635 mg) or incomplete responders (persistent AHR; PD 15 <635 mg). Results After six weeks of ICS, 11/46 patients (24%) had PIAHR. At baseline, incomplete responders had more severe AHR and higher type 2 (T2) biomarker levels including FeNO, blood- and sputum eosinophils as well as a higher density of airway chymase-positive mast cells. Despite reductions in T2 markers in both groups, incomplete responders exhibited higher blood- and sputum eosinophils after six weeks treatment. Airway mast cell and eosinophil densities decreased similarly, but reductions in blood eosinophils were smaller in incomplete responders. Conclusion PIAHR after six weeks of high-dose ICS is associated with incomplete suppression of T2 inflammation and mast cell-associated features. This pattern may help identify patients in whom airway inflammation is incompletely controlled by ICS alone and who may benefit from closer follow-up or further targeted treatment.

works.title: Persistent Pain in Pediatric Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Evidence for a Distinct Clinical Subtype
works.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, food antigen-driven inflammatory esophageal disease associated with diverse symptoms, including pain, which has received little attention. METHODS: We performed a retrospective, case-control study of 1,097 patients with EoE treated at Cincinnati Children's Hospital. Patients with documented, persistent EoE-associated pain were identified using a validated natural language processing algorithm. Following systematic review and abstraction of the electronic health record of patients with EoE-associated persistent pain (EoEp+) and no documented EoE-associated pain (EoEp-), a nested subgroup of confirmed subjects (n = 47 per group) was examined for clinical features and esophageal gene expression. RESULTS: Clinically significant EoEp+ represented 4.3% of EoE subjects. Demographics, disease activity including eosinophil levels, and dysphagia were similar between groups; however, patients with EoEp+ were older at initial presentation (13.01 vs. 7.997 years, p < 0.028). Within the EoEp+ phenotype, duration of EoE care is associated with increasing endoscopy burden over time (r = 0.68, p < 0.0001). Subjects with EoEp+ most commonly experienced abdominal pain-38% isolated pain and 62% with additional gastrointestinal symptoms-and experienced more polytherapy (p = 0.0020), treatment alteration (p = 0.027), and comorbid conditions than subjects with EoEp-. Gene expression analyses revealed decreased ALOX15 levels in EoEp+ esophageal biopsies, particularly in remission cases (p = 0.0062). CONCLUSIONS: Persistent pain in pediatric EoE is associated with a distinct clinical profile, characterized by greater treatment complexity, increased comorbid conditions, and dysregulated ALOX15 expression. These findings suggest that persistent pain in EoE identifies a clinically meaningful candidate endotype and highlights the need for targeted management strategies.

works.title: Dupilumab modulates type II IL-4/IL-13 receptor-expressing immune cells in eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis
works.journal: Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis (eCRS) is a refractory type 2 inflammatory disease characterized by nasal polyp formation and eosinophilic infiltration. Although dupilumab, an IL-4Rα-blocking antibody, demonstrates clinical efficacy, its cellular mechanisms within nasal polyps remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To define the cell type-specific effects of dupilumab in eCRS, we examined IL-4/IL-13 receptor-dependent transcriptional responses in tissue-resident immune cells. METHODS: Nasal polyp and peripheral blood samples were collected from five patients with eCRS before and after dupilumab treatment. Single-cell RNA sequencing on four paired cases, spatial transcriptomics, and immunostaining were performed. In vitro stimulation of human conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) validated IL-4/IL-13-regulated pathways. RESULTS: Dupilumab improved symptoms and attenuated eosinophilic inflammation. Across annotated populations, the number of differentially expressed genes correlated positively with pre-treatment IL13RA1 expression. Accordingly, myeloid cells, particularly cDCs, which predominantly express type II IL-4/IL-13 receptors, showed the broadest transcriptional changes, including downregulation of ALOX15; ALOX15 inhibition abrogated IL-4/IL-13-induced CCL13 and CCL22 expression in cDCs. After treatment, pathogenic Th2 cell subset expressed lower IL1RL1 and AREG. IGHE and IL4R expression in CD23-positive B cells declined, as did PRDM1 and ELL2 in plasma cells. In one paired case, spatial analysis identified fewer TLS-like aggregates and lower detection of ALOX15 and IGHE transcripts after treatment. CONCLUSION: Dupilumab preferentially remodels type II IL-4/IL-13 receptor-expressing immune cells, particularly polyp cDCs, while selectively reprogramming Th2, B, and plasma cells. Identification of ALOX15 as a candidate mediator in cDCs provides mechanistic insight that may inform optimization of type 2-targeted therapy in eCRS.

works.title: Mitochondrial DNA abundance is a determinant of immunogenic cell death in cancer
works.abstract: Cells experiencing mitochondrial stress can undergo apoptosis or cell death that triggers innate immune activation. We examined the mechanisms determining these distinct outcomes in cancer. Abundant mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and high expression of the cGAS-STING pathway were features of KRAS -mutant cancers. In a pharmacological screen, MEK inhibitor (MEKi) effectively induced mtDNA release into the cytosol in KRAS -mutant cancer cells. However, MEKi also induced PRKN-mediated mitophagy, which limited mtDNA release by eliminating damaged mitochondria. Inhibition of mitophagy sustained mtDNA efflux and amplified cGAS-STING signaling. Mechanistically, PRKN-mediated mitophagy restrained mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) to limit mtDNA efflux. The balance between mtDNA and cytochrome c (cyt. c ) release defined two immunologically distinct outcomes: immunogenic cell death (ICD) and apoptosis. In preclinical models, combined inhibition of MEK and mitophagy induced robust dendritic cell (DC) activation and promoted CD8 + T cell-mediated antitumor immunity. Consistently, PRKN expression negatively correlated with immune infiltration in human cancers. Collectively, these findings provide a rationale for combination strategies targeting mitochondrial dynamics to augment antitumor immunity.
